entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Ec(Jinning of the polemic part of the Epistle. The apostle bas finished his ta,k of self-vindicat.ion, and now proceeds in regular theological methOll to expound. ;rnd defend the <loctr1ne of justification' by faith without the deeds of the Lo.w. •• 0 foolish Galatians I who bewitched you, ••• before whose eyes Jesus Christ was evidently set forth in you, cruci\i_ed?" • I. THE APOSTLE'S SEVERE REPROOF. "0 foolish Galatians! who bewitched you?" Reproof is allowable and necessary, especially when it is prompted oy lcive to God and truth and by a tender interest in the welfare of men. 1. IJe point~ to the "witcheries" of the false tea,chers as the only way of accounting for the sudden and inexplicable change of sentiment in Gala'tia. There must have been some extrnordinary po\~er of delusion or of fascination at work to throw them so completely out of the line of Christian thought. Whether it was the witchery of logic or the witchery of sanctity, it was most effective in deluding the G,\lalians. 2. Th~ Galatians were "foolish" in ,1 ,'clr/ing to such ensnaring delusions. They were not answerable for tl,e conduct c,f their :1elu<lers, but tbcy showed an uncolllmuu 'folly. 'fhe Celtic natnre is quick, Lnt unstable. '!'he change was a senseless one. 148 THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. [OB, W, 1-29,

II. THE INEX0USABLENEss OF TIIEIR CONDUOT, "Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was evident.ly set forth in you, crucified." The apostle refers to his own clear exhibi- tion of gospel truth in Galatia, and especially to the individualizing distinctness with which the Redeemer was set before his converts as the only Hope of salvation. It was not only an exhibition, like a placard exhibited before their eyes, but it had its answering impression "within them." How, then, with such a view of Christ's person and work, could they have opened their minds to such destructive errors? III. THE TRUE THEME OF THE GOSPEL-CHillST CRU0IFIED. Naturalistic writers give us a Christ exalted far above the average altitude of men, but a man nevertheless • rationalistic writers give us a Christ as a leader of thought or as an example of self: sacri6ce and sympathy. "We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling-block, to the Greeks foolishness; but to them that are called, . . . Christ the Wisdom of God and the_ Po~er of God." The death o~ Ch_rist, as expressing the whole mystery of redemption, involved the whole matter In dispute. There could be no compatibility between Christ's cross and Jewish legalism. We can, therefore, well understand why the apostle resolved to know nothing in his preaching but Christ, and him crucified..

entries.title: GAL 3:2–5
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The apostle's first argument in this controversy. I. APPLICATION 011 THE TEST OF EXPERIENCE. "Received ye the Spirit by the works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith?" He begins by a practical test, which can be easily settled by experience and history. He refers to the time of awakening grace and :first love. 'l'hey had "received the Spirit." 1. He concedeS that they were Christians, though they were neither faithful, nor stable, nor sound. " The Holy Spirit is the characteristic posse5sion of believers." " If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." The reference may have been both to ordinary and extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. 2. He concedes that they were conscious of the possession of the Spirit. They had no occasion to ask him what he meant by their receiving the Spirit. Christian people ought to possess, not only a good hope through grace, but "a full assurance of hope." I!. THE RECEPTION OF THE SPIBIT POSSIBLE, NOT ON THE PRINCIPLE OF LAW, BUT OF GRACE. Though the Spirit was given under the Law, it was never given on a principle of Law, but it was under the gospel dispensation that it was given in Pente- costal power and abundance. No man ever yet received the Spirit, as the Author and Sustainer of the new life, by "the works of the Law," or by a course of obedience specially designed to work out salvation. Conspicuously, as to historic fact and inward experience, the Spirit was given to men in connection with the first promulgation of the "word of faith" at Pentecost. The Spirit was given " by the hearing of fait.h." "Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God." Yet the hearing that brings faiin with it is only possible through the Spirit's power, for many hear who do not believe, and therefore receive not the Spirit. There is no inconsistency here. We need the Spirit to enable us to believe, but the hearing is instrumentally necessary to our fuller reception of the Spirit. The apostle here, however, seems primarily to refer to the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, of which Peter spoke when he said that, after his preaching the Word," the Holy Ghost fell upon them as upon us at the beginning" (.Acts xL 15). Ill. THE DONATION OF THE SPIBIT IB NOT ON PRINCIPLE OF LAW, BUT OF GRACIP "He that ministereth to you the Spirit and worketb miracles in you, doeth he it by the works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith?" He first spoke of the reception, now he speaks of the donation of the Spirit : he :first referred to a particular point of time namely, their conversion; he now speaks of the principle ot' .God's continued actio'n. It is God who I!llllisters the Spirit--not the apostle-whether to work miracles of power or miracles of grace. But he does it, not on the principle of legal obedience, but on the principle of grace working through the instrumentality of the preached gospel He is "the God of grace," who sent his Son," full of grace and truth," to pour grace into iunumerable hearts. IV. THE FOLLY OF ATTEMl'TING TO BEGIN ON ONE PRIN0IPLE AND TO END ON ABO'l'Jl&B. "Aie ye so foolish? • having begun with the Spirit, are ye now being completed with the flesh?" This is folly, for it is to reverse the natural order of things. The opposites here are not Christianity and Judaism, but the essential and vital prillciple of each. If we begin our life with ~he Spirit1 it inus~ rc11ch i~s c,tt, tn. 1-29.] TlIE EPIS'fLE TO THE GALATIANS. 149

maturity with the Spirit. The Introduction of the flesh would be the annihilation of the Spirit. Judaism ministers to the sensuous element in our nature by making relil(ion a thing of rites and ceremonies; but this is to go back upon all the progress we have made in life, light, and blessing. v. 'l'HE USELESSNESS OF THEIB PAST BUFFERTNGS, "Did ye suffer 80 many things in vain ? if it be yet in vain." 1. It is a sign of sincerity to suffer for our opinions. There is no record in the Acts of a persecution in Gnlatia; but the Jewish element was strong enough there as elsewhere to resent by violence the contempt put upon their Law by the Gentiles being freed from it. There is a possible reference to these sufferings in the Epistle (eh. v. 11). 2. You stultify all your past sufferings if you rW!defrMA the gospel. All these sufferings represent so much wasted endurance or misery. 3. The apostle's reluctance to think their sufferings were in vain. "If it be yet in vain." He hopes better things of his converts. He knows that God keepeth the feet of his saints, so that they cannot altogether lose the things they have wrought.

entries.title: GAL 3:6–9
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Second argument-the case of Abraham. The natural answer to the previous question is" through the hearing of faith," and this as naturally s11:cgests the case of" faithful Abraham." The Jews boasted of their relationship to Abraham, and therefore an example taken from his history would have special force. I. THE JUSTIFICATION OF ABRAHAM WAS NOT THROUGH CIRCUMCISIO~, BUT BY FAITH. •• Even as Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness." No exception could be made to these words, for they were the very words of Moses (Gen. ::r.v. 6). The apostle dwells longer on the Old Testament, because the Judaists would naturally appeal to it. 1. Abraham was not accepted/or his virtues or his piety, or his circumcision, but because "be believed God, and it was counted to him for righteous- ness" (see homily on eh. ii. 16). His faith was accepted as righteousness, not as an act, for it had no merit in itself, but as a fact, for it was not by works, bat by faith, he was accepted. Bis faith was the mere instrument of bis justification, uot the ground of it; for Scripture always represents it as being" through" faith or" of" faith, never on account of it. 2. The transaction here referred to occurred hundreds of years before the Law was given on Sinai, and even some time before circumcision was appointed as a" seal of righteousness." If he, therefore, could be justified without circumcision, and prior to it, how then could the Judaists insist on its necessity? Abraham was not circumcised in order to be justified, but circumcised because be was justified. 3. The doctrine of the apostle was not, therefore, in any sense a novelty, aa the Judaista mighe think. It wuat least as old as Abraham. II. THE TRUE CONCEPTION OP ABRAHAMIO B0NBHIP, "Know ye therefore that they who are of faith, the same are sons of Abraham." 1. It is not Abraham's blood, but .Abraham's faith, which establishes the connection between the patriarch and his descendants. The Jews might say," We have Abraham to our father;" and they might ask in surprise, "What profit, then, is there in circumcision?" They would imitate bis circumcision rather than his faith. But the apostle says emphatically that the true sons are "they of faith," whose fundamental principle is faith. 2. It is Christ who makes the nexus between Abraham and us. We believe in Christ, who is Abraham's seed; therefore we are sons of Abraham. 3. There is but one Church in the t~ dispensations. Some modern sects hold that the Church is a. New Testament org:1nization, and that Old 'l'estament saints have no part in it. How can this be, ifwe believers "are blessed with "-not apart from-" faithful Abraham" ( eh. iii. 9)? The apostle shows bow Abraham has the heirship, the sonship, the kingdom, the glory, on the ground of the promise. He did not, therefore, receive the promise only for his children. Take the promise of the Spirit from Abraham; we take it from ourselves. Is the father of the family to be excluded, and only the children to gain admission to the kingdom? · III. 'l'HE PROOF FROM SORIPTURE. •• Moreover, the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the heathen through faith, announced the good news beforehand to Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed." 1. The exact import. of the promise, (1) 'l'he blessing is justification, which is oppo~cd to the curse of which be pre;ently speaks. llut that includes a title to eternal life as well as pardon. (2) 'l'he unity of Abraham and his spiritual descendants. He is the root and the repres~ntative of bi11 150 THE EPISTLE .TO THE GALATIA_NS, [on. m. 1-29,

see,l. The unity i~ not that established by circumcision, but something far deeper. 2, God had purposes of mercy toward the heathen, 'rhese purposes included their, justification on the same grounds as those which secured the acceptance of the Jews. 'The J~wish dispensation was particularistic, and was so far temporary and preparatory to a dispensation universalistic in its character, In Christ there was to be henceforth "neither Jew nor Gentile," 8. The way of salvation is the same in both d-ispensations. Old 'l'estament saints were saved exactly like New Testament &:lints, by faith in "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." The Levitical system was in itself an evangelical representation of the true method of salvation. 4. We .see here the value of Scripture/or proof,jor conjfrmation,jor comjo1·t, through all ages,. IV. CoMYUNITY AS WELL AS UNTI'Y IN THE BLESSING. "So then they whieh he. of faith are blessed together with the faithful Abraham." 1.. The blessing. It is the manifestation of Divine favour. The blessing and justification are regarded in the context as correlative terms. 2. The community between .Abraham and his seed. (1) He is" faithful Abraham," because of the simplicity, strength, and activity of his faith. He manifested all these characteristics of faith in (a) his self-expatriation; (b) his readiness to sacfifice Isaac; (c) his warlike courage; (d) his self-abnegation in the case of Lot. (2) He is the "fatLer of the faithful." There are but two properly representative men, the first and the second Adam; but Abraham holds a relation of his own, though not of a federal character, towards all who are his seed spiritually. He and they are blessed together. a. The ground of this community. It is the promise of God, "In thee shall the nations of the earth be blessed," realized in course of tim11 in the common faith of all who, whether Jew or Ge~tile, trust ~ pne Redeemer, and find in him their true inheritance as joint-heirs with him. ., .1

entries.title: GAL 3:10
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Third argument,-the curse of the Law. "For as many~ ar~ oftbework~. ef the Law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things written in the book of the Law to do them." 'rhe apostle is carried naturally by antithesis of thought from the blessing of faith to the curse-of the Law. I. THE CURSE. This is " the curse of the Law" of ver. 13, from which the Law- itself cannot deliver men, for its function is t0 condemn. 1. Jt is not the mere civil punish- men~ inflicted on the Israelites for the transgression of the ceremonial or judicial Law. The context shows that the curse is a far deeper thing, for the contra.tit.is.between wrath and blessing, condemnation and justification. Besides, the passage. refers to Gentiles who could not be affected by the dispensational peculiarities of Judaism. 2. Tlte curse is the Divine sentence upon transgressors involving doom and shame, the los~ of God, and separation from him ( Isa. lix. 2). The curse includes the penal sanction of the moral Law-a Law written in the hearts of Gentiles as it was delivered to Jews on tables of stone; so that Gentiles and Jews were alike under curse. It is a mistake; therefore, to regard the curse as the mere natural consequence of transgression, as di,;c-ase is the consequence of debauchery; it ie a penal evil. II. THE RANGE OF TBE CURSE, It extends to "as _many as are of the works of th, Law." A distinction is here necessary.between being of the works of the Law and being under the Law. The Old Testament saints were under the Law, but they were not under curse, because, like Abraham, they "saw the day of Christ afar off." They "believed God, and it was counted to -them for righteousness." They apprehended God's mercy and grace under the sacrificial forms of the Jewish economy. But the curse must necessarily descend upon "all who are of the works of the Law," because they have broken it and are still breaking it day by day. IIL How THE CURSE COMEB INTO OPERATION. It is by a Divine sentence which pronounces the curse upon all transgressors of the Law. The curse here quoted is the last of the twelve curses pronounced by the Levites on Mount Ebal (Deut. xxvii. 26). The reference points to ethical, not ceremonial, requirements. 1. '7'he Law demanils p,·actical obedience. It is not "hearers" of the Law, but "doers," who are in question. 2. lt demand6 a per6rmal obedience. " Every one." There is no room for a proxy or a mediator. 8. It def'Tl,Q/f/,IU a perfect obedience; for it covers" all the things written" in the Law. ¼. It must be a perpetual obedience, "Cursed is every one that continueth nut." The least failure involves the transgression of the whole Law (Jas. ii. 10).. ii. The ~Jfect <:f transgression i8 curse. All the evil that is iovolved in tl,nt terrible THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. 151

word. ••.D~th o.nd hell are the end of every sin, but not of every Rinner." 6. The Law slili exists to ·cursQ transgressors. It is not abrogated, though J u<laism is no more. Verp,. 11, 12.-Fourth. argument-the inconsistency of Law and faith. "But that DC\ man is justified in the Law in-the Hight of Goel, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith. But the Law is not of faith: but, The man that hath <lone these things ,hall live in them." • I. J US7'JFI<;lf'. 'fW~ JS 90'1'. op; THE SPHERE OF LA w. 1. Not because a perfect obed;ence would not bring iustification, for the fundamental principle of the Law is, "The man that hath done these things shall live in them" (Lev. xviii. 5). 2. But because no on~ is able to obey_p~.Law perfectly, Thus salvation becomes impossible on the principlr, of.Law. Il. SCRIPTURE ASSERTS THE CONNECTION OF JUSTIFICATION WITH FAITH, "The just shall ljve by. .faith." The apostle shqws the J udaists liow they misapprehended the doctrine of the Old Testament; for, several hundred years before Christ, the Prophet Habakkuk conn.ects life eternal with J~ith. "The Law is not of faith;" it does not find its starting-point in faith; doing, not believing, is the demand of the Law; and it is in no sense or manner connected with faith.

entries.title: GAL 3:13
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
..::..'Fifth argument-our salvation is by Christ ffl'Lde curse for us. Two thoughts are here brought into contr.ast-the Law condemned us; Christ redeemed Uij: "Christ redeemed' us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us." i. THE NATURE OF THE REDEMPTIOK, He "redeemed us." 1. This language does not counteruznce the theory that there was nothing in Christ's work but a mere deliverance from the power of sin. That is certainly involved in his death; for he came to "redeem us. froµi this present evil world" (eh. i. 4), and "to redeem us from all iniquity'' (Titus ii. 14). 2. Neither does it countenance. the idea that Christ redeemed us by entering into union with man and living a sinless human l_ife, which is reproduced in us by means of feHowship with him. Neither of these theories makes any provision for the rectification of man's relation with God, which is only effected through Christ being made a curse for us. II. How CHRIST ACHIEVED THE REDEMPTION. He "became a curse for us." This is an unfathomable thought. Yet let us try to interpret it in the light of Seri pture. We ar!l not redeemed by Christ's Divine doctrine, nor by his marvellous holiness of character, but by his entering into our very position before God, becoming" a curse for us." The Lord visited upon him what the Law awarded to us, and by that substitution our redemption was secured. We are not to suppose that the Son of God was less the object of Divine love n.t the very time that he was, in an official aspect as his righteous Servant, an object of Divine wrath. His Father always loved him. The assertion is made, first, that the curse of the Law rests upon transgressors; then, that we are liberated from .that curse; then, that this result was achieved by Christ becoming a curse for us. 'l'he passage shows what Christ was in God's account, not what he was in ,the eyes of men who despised him. III. How ms DEATH TOOK UPON IT THIS CIIARACTER OF CURSE. "For it is written, Cursed is every one that hangetb on a tree" (Deut. xxi. 22, 23). The allusion here is not specially to Christ, but to a command that those executed by Jewish law should not remain hanging on the tree all night. It does not refer to de.-ith by crucifixion, which was not a Jewish punishment, but to the exposure of the body after death, on crosses or stakes. But how was such a person accursed? Not because he was banged ution a tree, but he was hanged upon a tree because he was accursed. The apostle does not mean to attach the idea of shame to the mode of Christ's death; for he was not made a curse by his mere hanging on a tree, but he hung there because he was made II, curse for us. IV. 'l'HE ULTIMATE DESIGN OF THE REDEMPTION, "That'the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles in Christ." That is, the curse-bearing prepared the way for the blessin~, which was henceforth to stream forth upon the whole world. 1. The blessing wasJ°ustification of life, not mere temporal blessings, which were restricted to the Jews. 2. It was to reach the Gentiles" in Christ," who was made the curse for "us "-both "J,;ws and Gontiles"-not through the Law, whieh dcmaw.1~ e. perrect 1sa THE KPISTLE '1'0 THE GALATIANS. (t1D, lti. 1-29,

obedience. 3. It was designed for Gentiles as well as Jews. The stream WIii destined t.o flow through Jews to the Gentiles, freed from all the limitations of the old dispensation. V. THE nESULT OF THE BLESSING. " That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith." There is here an obvious return to the question of the aeoond verse, and a definite answer is now given to th:1t question, It was not through the Law, but through faith, we realize the promise of the Spirit. This was the special subject of promise (Joel ii. 28; Acts i. 4, 2; Eph. i. 13). Our Lord ha.s placed us in the dispensation of the Spirit, and has opened all blessings t.o men out of his arose and his tomb.

entries.title: GAL 3:15
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -.A newline ofargv:rMnt-tht relation between the covenant and the Law. Up to this point the apostle has touched upon no point that we have not seen in the Epistle to the Romans. Now he breaks new ground. "Brethren, I speak after the m:mner of men; Though it be but a man's covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man • disa.nnulleth, or ad<leth thereto." L IT IS ALLOWABLE TO USE HUMAN ANALOGIES Il!i ENFORCEMENT OF DIVINE TBUTII, The phrase, " after the manner of men," has various significations in the apostle's writings, bnt he evidently means here that the human analogy is perfectly appropriate, and that that which is true of a mere human arrangement is a fortiori of a.n arrangement made by God. II. THE CONDITIONS OF COVENANT-MAKING m HUMAN LIFE. 1. A covenant is an arrangement between two parties for mutual benefit, with an implied character of permanence. It is designed to perpetuate e. relation of some sort. 2. The covenant stands in the integrity of all its provisions without either party having the power to annul it or to add fresh clauses, whether consistent or inconsistent with its provisions. III. IMPLICATION THAT WHAT IS TBUE OF A HUMAN COVENANT 18 ESSENTIALLY INVOLVED m THE IDEA OF A DIVINE COVENANT. It is irreversible and irrevocable, since it is a covena.nt este.blished by oath. God swears and he will not repent. The Judaistic theory, however, under the form of e. supplement, would really effect the entire abrogation of the covenant.

entries.title: GAL 3:16
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -The contents of the covenant and the parties to it, "Now to Abrahe.m and bis seed were the promises made." L THE CONTENTS OF THE COVENANT. "The promises." They are elsewhere spoken or BI! "the promise." It was repeated several times. This promise carries the whole of se.lvation within it. It is elsewhere referred to as" the oath and the promise"-" the two immute.hle things in which it was impossible for God to lie''-for God confirmed the promise by an oath, e.nd the promise is linked with the Melchisedec priesthood of Christ, and thus involves all that is involved in priesthood, that is, e.tonement and intercession. It is the promise that bears up the burden of the world's hope, for it is on the ground of it we have "fled for refuge to the hope set before us" (Heb. vi. 18, 19). II. THE PARTIES TO THE ooVENANT. These are-God on the one side; Abraham and his seed on the other. Not Abraham a.lone, bnt Abraham and his seed. " And he saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." 'l'he seed was not the Jewish race, nor strictly the spiritual posterity of Abraham, but Christ himself, in whom the Jewish race found its embodiment and to whom the spiritual posterity was organically united. There is a distinction between Christ personal e.nd Christ mystical. regarded as the second Adam, as the Head of the body. 'l'hus we understand how the whole body of believers is expressly called "Christ" (1 Cor. xii.12). 'l'hey are "all one in Christ,'' and "if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed" (eh. v. 28, 29). - IIL A. :NECESSARY OONCLUSIOJr, H the seed is Christ, then the promise we.s not yet fulfilled, but awaiting fulfilment, when the Law was given. It could not, therefore, be disannulled by the Law, nor could the Law add fresh clauses to it.

entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The use and nature of the Law. "What then is the Law?" The apostle's reasoning seemed to make the Law a. quite superfluous thing. In the eyes of the J udaists it was God's most glorious institute. It was necessary, therefore, to show its nature, office, and characteristics, and its relation to the covenant of promise. It was really inferior to the dispensation of grace on four grounds, which themselves explain its nature a.nd use. I. THE LAw DISCOVERS BIN. " It was superadded because of transgressions." 1. It tDaS not to check sin. 2. Nor to create sin. 3. But to discover it. "By the Law is the knowledge of sin" (Rom. iii. 20). This discovery would necessarily multiply transgressions (Rom. v. 20), just as the introduction of light into a darkened room makes manifest the things that were before unseen. "I had not known sin but by the Law " (Rom. vii. 7). Many sins were not seen to be sins at all till the Law threw its intense light upon them. Thus the great service of the Law was to awaken conviction of sin in the heart and to make men feel their need of a. Saviour. The ceremonial and the moral Law had equally this effect. The system of sacrifice had no meaning apart from the fact of sin. What a. mistake, then, wa.s that of the J udaists who imagined that the Law could give them a title to eternal life in virtue of their obedience to its commands I II. 'l'E:E LAW WAS A TEMPORARY AND INTERMEDIATE DISPENSATION. "It was superadded ... till the seed shall have come to whom the promise has been made." '!'his refors to the coming of Christ who is" the Seed." The apostle puts himself back to the tirue of giving the Law, and looks forward from that starting-point to the future incarn[ltion. The Law was thus a mighty parenthesis coming in between Abraham's promise and the coming of the seed, and was specially preparative and disciplinary in relation to that future event. It was destined then to pass away as a dispensation, but the moral Law, which it held in its bosom, was to abide in its foll integrity. That La.w still exists in Christianity, with its old power of manifesting sin and carrying conviction to sinners so as to shut them up to Christ. III. THE LAW DID NOT OOJIIE DIBEOT FROM GoD TO lllAN, AS TIIE PROMISE CAME TO ABRAHAM, BUT THROUGH ANGELS BY A MEDIATOR. II Being ordained through angels ill the hand of a mediator." This is another point of inferiority. God gave the promise to Abraham immediately, not mediately by angels or through any intervention like that of Moses; unlike the Law, which was superadded through this double intervention. I. The share of angels in the giving of the Law. (1) Evidence of Scripture on the subject. Stephen says in his speech that the Israelites recoived the Law "at the ordinatiuu of angels," or "according to the arrangements of angels" (Acts vii. 53). 'l'he Law is eb~- 164 1'HE EPISTLE TO THE GA.J.ATIANS. [en. III, 1-20.

·where dr~crib~cl as "tl,c word ~poken by anp;els" (Ilch, ii. 2). Yet in tho history of tlie giving of the Law there is no reference to angels, not even to their prosence. In two passages their presence, but not their ministration, is referred to (Deut. xxxii. 2; Pa. b:nii. 17). (2) As the Law is said to have been ordained by means ofangeld and" the word spoken by angels," it is probable that the angels made it audible to the people or were connected with the terrible phenomena. which accompanied the giving of the Law. The angels ea.me between God and the people (Ps. lxviii. 17). (3) Tho presence of angels may have led in time to a perverted doctrine of angel-worship, against ,which the apostle warns the Colossians (Col. ii. 18). 2. The share of Moses in the giving of the Law. It was "ordained ... in the hand of a mediator," who wns Moses. He describes his own mediation: "I stood between you and the Lord at that time" (Deut. v. 6, ·2i). It was Moses who bore the tables of stone from God to the people. We are not to, suppose that the reference is designed to mark the inferiority of the Law. to the covenant of promise, which, too, had its Mediator, Jesus Christ the Lord. He is not coutra.s~itig the Law and the gospel, but the Law and the promise of Abraham; ap.d he asserts tJ:iat,' while in the one case the angels and Mosr.s had to do with its conveyance, God in the othr.r case gave the promise without the intervention of either man or angel; IV. THE LAW WAS DEPENDENT UPON CONDITIONS, TB;E PROMISE WAS ABSOLUTE, "Now, a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one." The very idea of mediation implies two parties, who are to be brought into some relation with each other through the inter'l"eotion of a third person. In the case of the Law, there were two parties-:--God and the Jewish people, In the case of the promise, "God is one;" he is mediatorless -no one stands between him and Abraham, as Moses stood between God and the Israelites in the giving of the Law. There is a numerical contrast between•'·' one" and "ofone." •

entries.title: GAL 3:21–25
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-TM Law d,esi_qned to·'be 811,bservient to the promise. Though the Law is inferior to the promise in the four points already suggested, it is not antagonistic to it. I. THE LAW IS NOT Al\'TAGONISTIC TO THE PROMISE. "Is the Law against the promises of God? God forbid." 1. The Law and the promise are equally of Divine origin';'--t1,1Jo distinct parts of the Divine plan, each part with its own distinct purpose to be carried out inside the Divine plan. The distinction between them is not tha~ the one is good and the other evil; for" the Law is good if a man use it lawfully," while. the promise is self-evidently and essentially so. 2. There would be antagonism if life came by the f,aw, ., For if there had been a Law given that could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the Law." In that case, the Law and the promise would have come into competition as two diverse methods of salvation. In the. one case, salvation would have come "of debt;" in the other case, it actually comes "of grace." If life came by the Law, there would, in fact, be no room for free gift at all. 3. The Law was absolutely incapabk of giving life. If it could have done so, it .would have been chosen as the method of salvation, because, in that case, man had only to use his faculties to accomplish it, and the agony of the cross would never have been necessary. I}ut the thing was impossible; salvation is a Divine work, and, if it comes at all, it mus~ come from the quickening power of the Spirit. 4. If.life could have come by the Law, its res1tlt, whi,ch is righteousness, would have come in the same way. But the. apostle has closed up the way of righteousness through the Law by many strong texts. II. THE TRUE EFFECT A:t."1> DESIGN OF THE LAW. "But the Scripture shut up all under sin, that the promise by faith in Christ might be given to them that believe." 1. Tl.e Law shuts up men u11der sin. The Scripture, rather than the Law, is here represented as doing it. It pronounces all to be guilty before God, but solely iP. virtue of the condemnation pronounced by the Law. 'l'he phrase here empl0yed is very expressive. Mim are as it were, closed in, or shut up, on every side, with only one way of escape-with no 'way left open but that of faith. 2. There is a gracious purpose in this legal, incarceration. "That the promise by faith in Christ might be given to them that believe." (1) '!'he blessing-" the promise," with all it involves. (2) 'l'he chaP.n~l of blessing- " faith." That is a precious conduit-pipe between the soul and the Saviour. ~3) 'l'he source of blessing-" Jesus Christ." (4) 1'he recipients-" them the.t believe.' !low t:'l"identl11 all blessing reaches us, not by the Law, but by grace I ill. THE J EWB IN WARD UNDEll THE OLD DlBPENSATIOll. "Ilut l:cfore faith came, "'" OD, m. l-r29.] THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS, 15,5

were kept under theLaw, shut np unto thEl faith which should nfterwar<ls be revealed." 1. The old dispensation described as the age '.' before the faith." (1) This does not mean tbot there.was bo faith in a, Redeemer in pre-Christian ages. To say otherwise is to say that there.,vae no salvation in those ages, The apostle ~hows elsewhere that Abrabl\m wee saved as Christiane ere now saved (Rom. iv.). (2) Pious Israelites lived "before the foi,th eame," because" the faith in him 88 really existent, or as Jesus, came with himself, into· the world." 2. The wardship of the Law in the old dispensrition. The apostle identifies himself with the whole body of believers under the old economy, anr\ represents• them· as under the strict surveillance of a rigorous janitor, who held them firmly under the discipline of the Law, with the design, however, that the very severity of their .bondage •might lead them to look·believingly for eseape to the Lord Jesus Obrist. 3. •The design of this wardship. "Shut up under the Law unto tbe faith which should afterwards be revealed." There was thus a gracious purpose in the very Law which was thus.,seen not to be "against the pr.omises of God." The Law still brings conviction of sin and shuts men up to the faith of Christ. It is not to be supposed" that the faith had not been revealed" from the earliest ages of the world-for Christ was the promised Seed to Adam-but there was a veil upon meu's minds till it was rent in the death of Christ. The faith revealed in due time was the faith of Christ incarnate. • lV.·TuE LAW OUB SCHOOLMASTER FOB OBRIST. "Wherefore the Law has become our tutor for Obrist, that we might be justified by faith." Thus we see bow "Christ becomes the end.of the Law for righteousness." 1. The symbolic ritual of the Law pointed expressly to Christ. "Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us." The sacrifices had no meaning apart from their typicn.l relationship to Christ. The Epistle to the Hebrews is the best commentary, on the Book of Leviticus. The Law with its sacrifices was always leading the Israelites to the" Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." 2. The moral Law wa.~ always leading to Ghrist; for it reveale<l sin, which deserved God's mighty condemnation. ·•3. The spiritual insufficiency of the Law was it, constant preparatirm of ths ,soul/or thefaith of Christ. •· Ver.,26.-The blessing of adoption. The apostle has already traced jnstification to faith, the inheritruice to faith, life to faith; now he traces adoption to faith. Believers are not children of Abraham merely, but sons of God. It is clear, then, that they are no longer children "in need of a schoolmaster." "For ye are all "-both Jews and Gentil~-" sons of God by faith in Christ Jesus." L i'l'HE FOUNDATION OF BONBHIP. 1. It o,riginates in the distingztishing grace of God., -We ".are·-predestinated to the adoption of children" (Eph. i. 4-6). 2. It is based· on the inoarnation, of the eternal San, who became. the Son of man that bis people might become the sons of God. The Father loves them in bis Son, and looks upon·them with the complacency.with whicb,he regards his Son. 3. It i's based on the mediatorial work of Christ; for, as it is in Christ "we have redemption through bis blood," so in him we "have obtaiaed the inheritance." Besides, God has sent forth his Son ·"to redeem them that were under the Law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" (eh. iv. 4,,5). -II. Tn.E -INB['BUMENT OF ADOPTION-FAITH. We become" sons of God by faith in Christ Jesus!' (John i. 12). It is clear, then, that we do not become sons of God by nature. 1. We are "by nature children of wrath." 2. We only become sons on believing. lIL· 'l'HE ADOPTION IS COMMON TO ALL BELIEVERS, WHETllEB JEW OR Gi,;NTILE, It· ie not enjoyed in a v1Lrying degree by believers, as some seem to think, as if God rcgnrded them with varying degrees of affection. "Beloved, now are we the :;ons of God;"·· 'l'he adoption carries with it Divine favour, discipline, training, tenderness, conformity to the image of God's Son. 1V, IT 18 A PRIVILEGE CONCERNING. WiiIOH BELIEVERS ARE NOT LEFT IN DOUDT; for-we receive the wituess of the Spirit that we arc children of God (Rom. viii. 16).

entries.title: GAL 3:27
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The import and obligationa of baptism. "For as many of you as wera baptized into Christ did put on Christ." !. THI!: IMPOltT OF BAPTISM IN'l'O CnrusT. 1. It declares our union with Christ. We &rt ba1itized into his death, so far os we partuke of it11 bcudit:;, and ore like hill\ TH:€ EPISTLE TO 'l'HE GALA'l'IANS. (on. nt. 1-29.

sepnrated from the world and ein. We are by bapt.ism separat.ed f'rom sin and devoted t.o Christ. 2. The fext does 'Tlot imply tliat all baptized pe,·sons have been baptized into Christ. Calvin well remarks that the apostle treats of the sacraments from two points of view. When he is arguing with hypocrites, he declares the emptiness of the outward ~bols encl .the folly of confidin~ in them. But in dealing with the case of believers, while he attnbutes nn false splendour to the sacraments, he refers emphatically to the inward fact signified by the outward ceremony. There is no warrant in this passage for the doctrine of baptismal regeneration, because the very persons here referred to were regenerated before they were baptized. Baptism followed upon their profession of faith in Christ. 11. THE OBLI(}ATIONS 01' BAPTISM. They did "put on Christ." Daptized into his death and buried with him in baptism, they rise with him into newness of life. They put on Christ like a cloak. The beauty of holiness is to be upon them, because they are "predestinated to the very image of Christ." The text is very expressive. 1. Christ is put on for a complete covering. Not merely as a girdle to the loins, but to enfold the whole manhood of believers. The idea is not that of protection from the coldnees' of an outside world, but that of the full adornment of Christian character. Believers are so to put on Ch1ist that the world may see Christ in the believer himself. 2. <Jhrist· ts put on for a constant covering. Not as a beautiful robe to be worn on high days and holidays, but on every day, in every scene of human life. 3. While believers are here represented as having put on Ghrist at their baptism, it is quite consistent for the' apostle to say," Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom. xiii. 12), and" Put on the, new man" (Eph. iv. 24). They are two sides of one great truth, representing in: the one case a change that was complete from the very beginning, and in the other a change that is incomplete, but in process of still further development. :

entries.title: GAL 3:28
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -.The tm,ity of 'believers. "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there Is neither bond nor free, there is not male and female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." I. IT IB AN ORGANIC tn."ITY. Believers are "one body in Christ" (Rom. xii. 4, 5); "one man;" "one new man" (Eph. ii. 15). The unity in question is no ecclesiastical unity; for it joins together those who are ecclesiastically separated, and it connects. together the believers of all generations. 1. It has a sevenfold relationship. "There . is one body, and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one hope of your calling, one God and Father of all" (Epb. iv. 4-6). 2. lt 'is created in <Jhrist by the • Holy Spirit. It is Christ, not the Spirit, who "bath made both one" (Eph. ii. 14) ; and we, " being many, are made one body in Christ" (Rom. xii. 5). But wherever the , Spirit is there is union with Christ. The indwelling of the Spirit is therefore the bond of unity in the Church. II. JT IS A UNITY WHICH OBLITERATES OB lGNORl!:B MANY WORLDLY OR NATURAL· J>IBTINCTIONB. All distinctions, whether of condition, or nature, or sex, are in Christ , lost sight of or forgotten. 1. National distinctions. "'l'here is neither Jew. nor' Greek." This distinction meant much in pre-Chlistian ages. The Jews were God's peculiar people, blessed with great privileges and prepared for great destinies. The • Greeks, representing the Gentile world, stood apart from the Jews-" aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise" (Eph. ii.12). But · Jew and Greek stand on exactly the same footing in the kingdom of Go<l, possessed of equal privilege, equally sone of God, and equally heirs of God. Christ broke down . the middle wall of partition that severed them for ages, and made them one commonwealth. 2. Distinction, of human station. "There is neither bond nor free." Slaves· were excluded from certain rites of heathen worship. But Christ takes the slave by the hand and places him in his kingdom side by side with the free man. 'l'he largest body of practical counsel in the apostolic Epistles is directed to slaves. 3. The dift~nc- . tum of sex. "There is not male and female." The apostle does not touch the ongmal subordination of the woman to the man, which is a still existing fact (1 Tim. ii. 11-14), but shows how reli,.,iously regarded, men and women are equal. Their relation to Christ does not'dest~y the old fact, but causes it to be lost sight of. Ho.w true it is that Cbristiauity alone has elevated women, has created the sentiment which dest:oys slavery everywhere, u.nd creates a better understanding among tile nution11 of tho world! • O'EI, DL 1-29,] THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. 157

entries.title: GAL 3:29
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -The lieirs. "And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise." Mark how the apostle moves from point to point. I. BELIEVERS ARE CHRIBT's POSSESSION. They are so : 1. By gift. " Thine they wero, and thou go.vest them me" (John xvii. 6). 2. By purchase. "Ye are bouaht with e. price" (1 Cor. vi. 20). 3. By conquest. "The people shall be willing in the day of thy power" (Pe. ex. 3). 4. By their own self-surrender. They are "a living sacrifice." 'rhey have "committed themselves to him" (2 Tim. i. 12). II. CHRIST'S PEOPLE ABE ABRAHAM'S SEED, Christ himself is Abraham's Seed (ver. 16), and therefore they, as one with him in the mystical union, are Abraham's seed. III. THE HEmSHIP OF PROMISE. They became heirs, not by any legal observances, but according to the promise made to Abraham. 1. The inheritance is the only one worth having. 2. It is the only one that can he kept for ever. 3. It is, unlike earthly riches or honours, within everybody's reach. 4. It is the duty of heirs to live accordina to their prospects, to walk worthy of a Father's house, and to behave like a brothe; to brethren.

entries.title: GAL 3:1–14
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The bewitchery of Law. Paul, having stated his position as dead to the Law and inspired by Christ, goes on in the present paragraph to appeal to the Galatians to free themselves from the bewitching power of Law, and to yield themselves to the faith in a crucified and now risen Christ, which alone secures justification and its cognate blessings. And here we notice- I. How LAW OAN COMPETE SUCCESSFULLY WITH A CRUCIFIED SAVIOUR FOR 1"HE HOMAGE OF TIIOUGHTLESS HEARTS. (Ver. 1.) Paul here declares that two attractive powers had been presented to the Galatians-a crucified Christ in his own preaching, and the Law in the preaching of the Judaizers; and, to his amazement, the Law had so bewitched them' as to lead them to look for salvation to Law-keeping instead of to the Saviour, And yet it only brings out the fact that there is in Law and selfrighteousness a bewitchery which is continually leading souls back to bondage. It seems so natural to establish some claim by Law-kee!Jing and ceremony that poor souls are from time to time falling into legal hope and its delusions. The superstition, which is abroad now, and leads so many to ceremonials for salvation, rests upon this foundation. It is the fascination of an evil eye which is upon the foolish votaries; they fancy they can save themselves by Law, and maintain their self-complacency and pride all the time. But it is delusion pure and simple. II. ALL THAT LAW CAN REALLY DO FOB SINNERS lSTO CONDEMN THEM. (Vers.10, 13.) The position taken up by Law is this-to condemn every one who falls short of perfect obedience. No partial obedience will be entertained for a moment. "Every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the Law to do them," is by the Law "cursed." This tremendous deliverance ought to be the death of all "legal hope." The soul who continues to hope in the Law, after such o. definite utterance only proclaims his foolishness. One breach of Law is sufficient to secure the curse. The Le.w maintains its demand for perfect obedience, and, if this be not rendered, it can do nothing but condemn. It becomes the more a.me.zing that any after this coulu be bewitched by Law. Surely if the Law can only curse sinners, the sooner we look for salvation in some other direction than Law, the better. And to go back to Law-keeping; from grace, in hope of acceptance, is clear retrogression. III. JUSTIFICATION AND ITS COGNATE BLESSINGS CAN ONLY COME BY FAITH. (Vers. 2- 9, 12, 14.) 'l'he Law in the nature of things cannot justify sinners. It has no means of doincr so. But God in his grace has provided o. way of justification. It is through the me~its of his Son, And here we must remember that imputation if merit is the commonest fa.et of experience. 'fhere is not one of us who does not get a start in life and a consideration extended to us which are duo to the merits of others, a respected parent or some deeply interested friend. We are surrounded with o. halo of glory by virtue of the character of others. Their ch11racter helps us to a position and opportunity we could not otherwise obtain, It me.y be co.lied e. nicre associ11tion of ideas, but it i$ 158 THE EPI'STLE 'l'O THE GALATIANS. [OJI, JU, 1.-29,

strictly the pasi:ing of merit ovtlr from man to man. In the sl\me way Jesus Christ has come into our world, allied himself with olll' sinful race, meriteu consideration and acceptance by obedience to L&w, even as far 88 death, and this merit of the Divine Man passes over to believers, In the Father's sight, therefore, we are regarded as just, notwithstanding all our sin, We have been justified through faith,. But besides, the believers obtain the Spirit to dwell within them, so that a process of 11anctifioo.tiou is set up within them 88 soon as justification takes place. And the indwelling Spirit may manifest his presence and power in wonderful works, as appears to hove been the case with these Galatfans (ver. 5). So that Divine grace not only secures the' jo.sti:fi-' cation of all who trust in Jesus, but their sanctification and spiritual power 88 well, Wondrous blessings are thus the outcome of Divine grace, 11,nd the heritage of those who believe. \Vhat a change from having to endure the curse of Law I , 1· i. , IV. ABRAHAM ILLUSTRATES THE BENEFIT OF FAITH IN Goo AS CONTRASTED WITH RELIANCE ON LAw. (V ers. 6-9.) The legalists claimed Abraham as their father. One, woulu have supposed that Abraham had been the greatest ceremonia.list of the early dispensation. But the truth is that Abraham was justified and accepted by simply believing God when he promised a world-wide blessing through Abraham's seed. The blessing came t-0 the patriarch through simple trust in God. Those who hoped in Law-keeping, therefore, were not the true followers of Abraham. It was only those who trusted God for salvation and blessing who walked in the patriarch's footsteps. Consequently, all the ceremonialism which tried to shelter itself under the :wings· of Abraham.was a simple imposition! The" merit-mongers," as Luther calls them in his' Commentary,' have thus no pretence ofcoun tenance Crom the case of Abrabam. . It was to simple trust.in God Le owed his standing before him. How needful, then, it is for us to shake. ourselves. free from every remnant of self-righteousness, and to look simply and implicitly to Christ alone I It is by faith we stand and live. The Christ who became the curse for us by hanging on a tree, calls us to trust him for acceptance and inspiration; and in trusting him we find the promise amply redeemed.-R. M. E. •

entries.title: GAL 3:15–22
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Thecovenant of promis,e. Having taken up the case of Abraham as illustrating the necessity of faith, Paul proceeds to state the Abrahamic covenant ai1 one of promise. 'l'he Mosaic covenant, promulgated four hundred and thirty years after. could not, he argues, disannul the previous covenant. It must have a supplementary rurpose; and this he shows to be to drive the souls ,vho have been made hopeless b_v the Law into the arms of the "faithful Promiser." The following lessons arii sug, gc8ted :- , :: I. THE COVENANT OF PROMISE IIIADE WITH CHBIBT AS SEED OF ABRAHAM. (Vers.15, l G,) We are too prone to contemplate the promises of God out of their relation to Christ.: No wonder that they then seem incredible. They are too good news to .be true,· But the uceeding great and precious promises are all yea and amen in Christ (2 Oor, i. 20) ; they are promises made to Christ and secured by his obedience; a)ld consequently they ought not to seem at any time incredible. Now, when God spoke to Abraham of a nniversal blessing being given through the patriarch's" Seed," it never su!!gested t<), Abraham any idea of merit upon his part. He simply µoped upon .God's word, whioh would be fulfilled in due season. The Seed would convey the blessing, The old man,'11 hope rested upon his Seed, the Christ whom the ages would reveal. The Seed might.,be meritoriou.s, but Abraham felt that he himself was not. In the humility .of felt helplessness, therefore, he trusted God, and found pardon and acceptance and inspil'ation tl,rouah bis trust. It is just Lere we must all begin. The Lord J,esus deserves the fulfilr:;ent of all the 1,romises. The covenant of grace made with him by the Father has received a fulfilu;ent of its conditions so far as he was concerned; and s~ •he, can claim the promises as no more than his due. '!'heir guarantee is in his obedience ,unt,1 dc:alh. , . II. THE SINAITIO LAW 00ULD NOT DISANNUL THE COVE;NAKT OF PBOMISr:.' (Vere, 17, 18.) Four hundred and thirty years elapsed and, lo, another cove)lp,nt is ma.de with the seed of Abraham. At Sinai, and through the mediation of Moses and of angels, a "fiery Law" went forth from Heaven, .and the question Paul answers here is what effect this latter covenant had upon the former. He a-i<luces the fact that legal documeut~ 11·he11 onc4' 1,crfocbl are not disauuullcd by tiUb~C(!llCilt onl's. 'fhe lattir Oil, III, 1-20.] THE EPISTLE 'fO THE GALATI.AXS. 150

doouments must proceed upon tho validity and power of the preceding, Hence the MosELic LELw could not render the Abrahamic covenant of promise null and void. It must consist with and supplement the preceding. The promise made to the seed of Abraham remained in force, notwithstanding the thunders of Mount Sinai. Nay, tho thunders of Sinai were, as we shall next see, to incline the people to accept the previous promise. There was no antithesis between promise and Law; but Law came to incline the people to embrace the promise. There was something more veneraole and more sacred even than the covenant at Sinai, and this was the promises made to Abraham in Canaan. 'l'heso were the well-head of Jewish privileges. The Jews had not been called to law-keeping and self-righteousness, but to promises exceeding great and precious to be won by,their Messiah. It was to faith, not to ceremony, that their system really summoned them; Ill. THE-PURPOSE OF THE LAW. (Vers.19-22.) Was the Sina.itic covenant, then, e. work of ·supererogation? By no means. It was a grand instrument, when rightly regarded, to drive sinners into a Saviour's arms. What did it require? Perfect obe- ·dience. Did the·people at Mount Sinai fancy they could renderit? Nay; the utterance of the ten commandments in the great and terrible tones convinced them that they could not stand up in their own strength before such a holy God. Hence their flight from the mount (Exod. xx. 18). Hence their cry for the mediation of Moses (ver. 19). In a. word, the effect of the publication of the Law was to overwhelm the people with a sense of their sin. This is the purpose of the Law. It. is not to feed man's hope of claiming life by law-keeping; it is, on the contrary, to kill that hope and send him to God's free grace that be may be saved by faith in the promises. The Law is to secure our despair of self that we may build all our hope on the Saviour. What, then, were the ceremonies of Judaism? They were embodiments of the promises. The Judaizers said," We a.re to be saved by observing these ceremonies;," but the truth was that the ceremonies were enacted to make the promises emphatic and to lead sinners away from self-righteousness to God and his mercy. The ceremouial Law was a pictorial gospel, to keep up the hearts of those whom the moral Law had reduced to <lespair; but the false teachers ma.de the ceremonies saving, and so ignored the gospel they embodied. May we be kept from all analogous mistakes !-R. M. E.

entries.title: GAL 3:23–29
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The Law-school and the hom&-coming. Paul, in the present section, pursues the thought of the purpose of Law. It is the tutor to convey certain lessons to the soul and to secure thereby the soul's return to the Father and the home. Let us look at the interesting line of thought thus given. I. 'l'HE LAW-SCHOOL. (Vers. 23, 24.) The idea was once entertained that the Law, as ,rcz,1icz')'"")'Os, meant the slave who was entrusted with the guidance of the child to the school of Christ. But this notion is now abandoned, and, as the superior slaves were oft-en entrusted with the education of the child to a certain age, the idea which is now accepted from this passage is that the soul goes to the school of the Law, und learns from the Law the lessons which fit it for coming home to Christ. Christ is not the Schoolmaster to whom Law leads the soul, but is the elder Brother of the Divine family to whom the lessons of the schoolmaster, the Law, leads the enlightened soul. The Lawschool is an institution of great strictness and severity. Hence we are represented here as "kept in ward under the Law" (Revised Version). Like one of the great barracks which am called euphoniously "public schools," o.nd where, as in public prisons, the youths a.re for some hours daily confined, and out of which they are thankful to escape; so the Mosaic Law is meant to be the severe training-school which will make us relish ever so much the freedom and comfort of home. II. 'l'HE BURDEN OF ITS TEACHING. (Ver. 24.) The lesson of the Law is personal unworthiness, the impossibility of our ever saving ourselves. 'l'he more we study the ten commandments, the more we enter into the spirit and meaning of the moral Law, the deeper must be our conviction that we cannut keep it perfectly, and so must be liable to its penalties. But the Jews, instead of holding hard to the teaching of the moral Law, turned their back upon it and betook themselves to the cll'l'emoniaZ Law as their hope of life. '!'heir notion was that, though they might neglect the weightier mntters of the Law, such o.s judgment, mercy, and faith, they were perfectly Rafe so Ion~ as tllcy tithed the mint, tho anise, and the cuwmin (MMt. xxiii. 23). Instead of learn- IGO THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE GALA.'l'IANS. [CH, III, 1-29,

ing Law's lesson and being "shut up to faith," they mistook the lesson altogether and sbut t.bem~clves up to ceremony. The Law was meant to defuat self-righteousness; the pupil_s all~wed it to minister to self-righteousness. Instead of being shut up to fe.ith, they reme.med m the school of Law for ever and never got home. Now, every well-conduoted school impresses upon its pupils the desirability of their getting beyond its lessons e.nd its confinement. 'l'he broad liberty of manhood and of home lies in supposed sunlicrht beyond it, and the school training encot1rages the vision. So with God's Law • it is designed to create a longing for the liberty in Christ and the larger opportunitie~ that liberty implies. Ill THE HOME-COMING. (Vers. 25, 26.) If we learn the true lesson from the Law we are carried by it to the feet of Christ, and we seek justifice.tion by trusting him: Faith is thus the home-coming of the soul ; and undoubtedly no schoolboy ever co.me whistling so joyfully home, even when his home-coming was the final one, as the soul does which has learned to trust and love Christ. Then the sense of imprisonment and confinement gives place to a sense of freedom. AB children of God in Christ Jesus we rejoice in the abundant liberty of home. Our education is so fer finished when w~ have learned to hope in our elder Brother only. Then do we know what it is to be "at home" with God. The prodigal son enjoyed himself greatly at the father's banquet, and so do all of us; for we are all prodigals by nature, when by faith and repentance we come home to God. IV. U1-."ITY IN CHRIST. (Vers. 27, 28.) The home-coming is attended by the enter- tainment of the Christian spirit. By that spirit all caste-distinctions die. Havincr put on Christ, we do not look contemptuously on any, but hopefully on a.II. The Je; and the Greek forget their national differences and separations ; the bond and the free do not dwell despairingly or proudly on the accident of birth; the man does not tyrannize over the woman, and neither will the Christian woman, when she secures her rights, t_,rannize over the man ; but each and all will rejoice in their unity in Christ. Christ thus proves himself to be the unifying element in the human race. Coming near to each, he brings ea.eh near to all, and establishes around his person the brotherhood of man. V. FAITH ALSO INTRODUCES SOULS TO THE PRIVILEGES OF THE AllRARAMIO FAMILY, (Ver. 29.) Unquestionably the Jews were the heirs of magnificent promises. But is it carnal Jews that are to get them? is it men who a.re only descended from Abraham according to the :flesh? :Nay; Abraham has a spiritual seed, and all who a.re Christ's through faith become children of Abraham. Paul thus proclaims a chosen generation, whose fellowship may be entered by faith and not by circumcision, by the Christian spirit and not by Jewish ceremony. This is better than converting the world to Judaism, to convert it to Christ, and through relationship to Christ to count kindred with Abraham. " We are the circumcision," as be says to the Philippian converts, "who worship God in the spirit, who rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the :flesh" (Phil iii. 3). '.!.'he Law teaches us a precious lesson if it sends us for salvation to Christ, and enables us to find in fellowship with our Lord the privileges of the chosen people becoming ours.-R. M. E.

entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Appeal to experienc,e and Scriptwre. I. FooLISRNEBB OF THE GALATIANS aHOWN FBOK TREIB OWN EXPERIENCE. 1. Expression of astonishment in view of their first impressions of the cross. "0 foolish Galatians, who <lid bewitch you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly set forth crucified ? " Paul's address to Peter concluded with his presenting the dreadful supposition of Christ having died for nought. He with that turns to the Galatians, and calls to their recollection the memorable impression which the first presentation of Christ crucified had made on their; minds. There had been, as it were, a localization of the cross among them. Christ had been so presented to them that preacher and time and place were all forgotten. There on Galstian soil was the cross erected; there was the Holy One and the Just taken and nailed to the tree ; there his blood flowed forth for the remission of sins. And they were deeply affected, as if the crucifixion scene had passed before their eyes. It is a blessed fa.et that the evil of our nature is not insuperable-that there is in the cross what can act on it like a spell. Even the greatest sinners have been arrested and entra.uced by the eye of the Cruci.Jied One. It is, on the other hand, a serious fact that OR. III, 1-2!),] THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. 181

evil can be presented to us in a fascinating form. Here the Galatians a.re described as those who ha.d been bewitched. H wa.s as if some one had exerted an evil spell on them. Hie evil eye had rested on them and held them BO that they could not see him by whose crucifixion they had formerly been BO much affected. And the apostle wonders who it could be tha.t had bewitched them. Who had been envious of the influence which the Crucified One had obtained over them? What false representations had he made? What flattering promises bad be held out? Such a one had grea.i guilt on his head ; but they also were chargeable with foolishness in a.llowincr tbemseltes to be bewitched by him. The Galatians were by no means stupid; they were rather of quick perception. They had the strong emotional qualities of the Celtic nature_; their tei:npt3:tion was s?dd~n cban~e of feeling. They _were foolish in yielding to their temptation, m not subJectmg theu feelings to the guidance of reason, in not using the Divine helps against their being bewitched. And the apostle, in cbaro-ing home foolishness on them, would have them recall what the cross had once bee~ in their eyes, in order to break the present spell of evil 2. The one admission he aJJks of them in order to prove their foolishness. "This only would I learn from you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith?" He felt that he had such a hold on them from their past experiences that he could have asked of them many admissions. With one, however, be will be content. This bad reference to the reception of the Spirit. The gospel dispensation was the dispensation of the Spirit. It was by the sacrifice of Christ that the Spirit was really obtained. It was soon after the offering of that sacrifice that the Spirit was poured out, as though liberated from previous restraints. The great blessing, then, of that dispensation, obtained they it by the works of the Law, or by the bearing of faith? The Law is to be understood in the sense of the Mosaic Law, which the Judaists sought to impose on Gentile Christians. The Law and faith are here placed in opposition. Works are the characteristic of the Law; bearing is the characteristic of faith. Was it, then, by Law-working that they had received the Spirit? When would it quantitatively and qualitatively have sufficed for their receiving the Spirit? Was it not the case, too, that the great majority of them in the Galatian Churches bad not been under the Law? They had not been circumcised, and yet the Spirit bad been received by them. Was it not, then, by the hearing which belongs to faith? They had not tediously to elaborate a Law-righteousness. They had not to work for a righteousness at all They had simply to hear in connection with the preaching of the gospel. They bad to listen to the proclamation of a right- eousness elaborated for them. And while their faith was imperfect, and could not be in itself the ground of their justification, they had, as perfectly justified, received the Spirit. 3. 7'wo points in which their foolishness was shown at its height. "Are ye so foolish ? " (1). They belied the beginning they had made. "Having begun in the Spirit, are ye now perfected in the flesh?" They began by renouncing the flesh, by confessing that, with the weak elements in their nature, they never could arrive at perfection. In despair of the flesh, then, and in order to be delivered from its weakness, they cast themselves upon the Spirit. They called in Divine help against their sinful tendencies. This was the right beginning to make. And having thus begun, they should have gone on, i11 dependence on the help of the Spirit, toward perfection. But they were proving untrue to the beglnning they bad made. They were going back to the flesh which they professed to have left behind as a source of dependence. 'fhey were now saying tbat it, forsooth, with all its weakness, was able to bring about their perfection. (2) They stultified their sufferings. " Did ye suffer so many things in vain? if it be indeed in vain." It ls to be inferred that they suffered persecution. They suffered many things, though of their sufferings we have no record. They suffered for ChriRt, and it may have been for liberty in him. That gave a noble character to their sufferings, and promised a glorious reward. But now, with their changed relation to Christ, those sufferings had lost their character. There was no longer a Christian halo around them. They were simply a blunder, what might have been avoided. They could not hope, then, for the reward of the Christian confessor or martyr. The apostle is, ho~ever, unwilling to believe that the matter has ended with them. In the words which he appends, "if it be indeed in vain," he not only leaves a loophole of doubt, but mak_es _an appeal to them not to throw away that which they bad nobly won. 4. The one admissitlt' reverted to with special rrference to the miraculous operations of the Spirit. "He therefore GALATIANS, II lGJ TUE EPISTLE ,TO '£.ij.E,:GALA'J:IA,N~.

that supplieth to you the Spirit, an,l w,,rketh miracles among you, doeth ho H by ~ho works of the Law, or by the henring of faith?" It was G9d who supplied the Spirit to them. There could be no question regarding the hial) authority of Abrabam'.s example. And the best way to deal with it was in connec~qn with Scripture. What, then, ~as the Scripture account, of 4,br~h::im's jus\ifica.tion? ,Iii Gen. xv. 6 it is said, " He believed in the Lord, and he counted it to him for. rigb teoui:;7 ness."
