entries.title: GAL 5:12
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -,-Afierce.stroke of apostolic irony, The apostle had been so profoundly stirred by the false accusations of the J udaizers and their fanatical zeal for circumcision, which- was, after •all, a mere " glorying in the flesh," that he throw11 out a wish that those •who were trying to unhinge Galatian Christianity would themselves exemplify this" g!.:>rying" to the extent that was so familiar among the worshippers of Cybele at Pessinus, one of the towns of Galatia. His readers would have no difficulty in understanding the allusion. If. circumcision was good, the priests of Cybele had somethin~ better to offer. It ;,vas.a piece of contemptuous sarcasm, which exhibits the passionate feeling of the apostle caused by their unceasing effort.a to undermine the gospel for the sake.of a. ~ere mark in the flesh.

entries.title: GAL 5:13
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Tlie meaning of Christian liberty. • The false teachers deserve this severity of treatment, for they would deprive you of your liberty. I. THE CHBISTI:AN CALLING IS TO LIBERTY. He had already counselled them to stand fast in the liberty wherew:ith Christ had. mllde them free (ver. l}-a liberty which lifted them out of legal bondage, and, above all, destroyed the yoke of ancient ceremonialism ; and ,now these .Judaizers were attempting to strike at the root of their calling. II. THE DEEP AND UNCHANGEABLE DISTINCTION BETWEEN LIBERTY AND LICENTIOUS- NESS, •~only use not liberty for an occasion to the fiesh." This counsel was specially needed Jor a Celtic people emerging out. of the old immoral. paganism. It shows: 1. That duty is 'Tlot destroyed by liberty. '£heir escape• from legal bondage did not involve the annihilation of all moral restraints or the abrogation of the moral Law. In fact, the grusp,el bring11.,,believ:ers under a weightier obligation to duty than the Law possibly can do,,for it brings upon th11: believer the mighty constraint of Divine love (2 Cor. v. 14),, :They were no longer justified by the Law, but the Law was still a rule of life. The_>4'ntinomians of Germany and England held that .believers were under Law in no· sense,; that they were ;under no obligations to obedience; and therefore were ready enough.to use,their liberty under the gospel" for an occasion to the flesh." It is still very necessary to emphasize ;he obligations of Christian people under the gospel, for gross immoralities have been committed by men with an extravagant view of gospel liberty. Christ ea.me to call sinners to repentance, not to licentiousness; to take his yoke upon. them, .and yield their members instruments of righteousness unto holiness. 2. Christian people ought to use their liberty wisely. There is a margin left for human discretion in the application .of gospel principles. Perhaps a too free use of our Christian liberty has ,often. become an occasion of sin. Therefore a Christian divine suggests that in.matter!! of duty .we ought to do too much rather than too little, but in matters of indifference we should rather take too little of our liberty than too much. Ill. Tl!E ONLY. BOlH)AGE ALLOWABLE,J:N CHRISTIANITY IS MUTUAL LOVE. "But by love serve one another." There is an antithetic force in the original, which is not so ol;,vious )l1 the translation : If you must. have bondage, let it be the bondage of mutual lQY\I, , Love is to be. the means. by which the mutual bondage is to be manifested. 1. Tkis,~Q'fl,dage is not degrading, Though they, were servants of each other, they wern not•.masters of each other, "All ye are brl!thren." Christ himself is our example in this service : 0 1 am 1;1.mong you as one that serveth." This one fact lifts this duty to an incomparable height of dignity and impressiveness. 2. It is tJ.is which will keep your. liberty/ram r!,,egenerating into lice1,tiousness. Their love for one another, grounded in their love for God, would set them upon all opportune ways of benefiting ea.eh other. 'l'hus love is the one deb,t always to be discharged and .always due. "Owe no mau 272 THE EPISTLE TO THE GALA'l'IANS. [oH, '\>, 1-26,

anything, but to love one another" (Rom. xiii. 8). The counsel of the apostle seems to suggest the existence in Ga.Jatia of factious quarrels and unchristian isolations.

entries.title: GAL 5:14
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -The spirit of the Law. Mutual service was only possible 'through·rnutual 1ove, and this love was exp!'essly commanded in the Law, which says," 'l'hou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." I. WHAT IS THE LAW WHIOB FINDS ITS FULFil,lllENT IN LOVE? It is not the law of Christ, nor the law of libertr, nor the law of the Spirit of life, but the very Law of which the apostle has been spea.krng all through the Epistle. His readers could •not have understood him if he had used the term "Law" in a -different sense. It follows, therefore that the Law must still be in force, because its essential commandment, love, remain~ for perpetual fulfilment. Love was always, even in Old 'restament times, the fulfil- ment of the Law. The sum of the Decalogue is love (Matt. xxii. 40). The apostle says, "He that loveth another hatb fulfilled the Law" (Rom. xiii. 8, 9); but this does not imply, as Antinomians say, that if we have love we have nothing to do with the Law. Believers are exhorted, in the 1iassage quoted, to love one another 9n the ground of its being a requirement of the Law. It is absurd, then, for the Antinomians to talk of love as being higher than Law, for love is just the fulfilling of the Law, and nothing more. A perfect love would keep the whole Law. It ·is, therefore, absurd for Roman Catholics to affirm tha.t love justifies as well a.s faith, because love fulfils the Law. Sin hinders the perfection of our obedience, and therefore love cannot. perfectly fulfil the Law. IL How LOVING oUB 1'"EIGHBOUB FULFILS THE LAw: It is the wa.nt·oflove tha.tleads men to commit murder, adultery, theft, false witness. If we rightly loved our neigh- bour, these sins would be impossible. But.we cannot rightly Jove our neighbour till,we have loved God. " He that loveth not his brother whom he .bath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" "This is the love of.God, that (f11a) we may keep his commandments." 'l'here is a necessary connection between love to God and love to our neighbour (1 Cor. viii. 1-3). III. THERE IS NOTHING-HIGHER IN THE SPHERE OF DUTY TRAN THIS LOVE, The Posi- tivists assume that they have discovered in" altruism" a. principle higher than· either Law or gospel ever taught. Whereas we a.re commanded in Scripture to love our neighbour a.s ourselves, the Positivists say that we ought to love him better than ourselves. We are to deny ourselves for the sake of others. This is Christ's idea.; but, if there be no future life, it would be the mark of a. fool, and· not of ,a. hero; to .deny myself for anybody. The idea. of altruism, however, fails to realize itself in the lives of Positivists. Besides, if one's own happiness ought not to be a. good to himself, there is no reason why ·he should secure happiness for another. In· a. few yea.re it will make no difference to me what I have been, whether I have practised altruism or not. The "·orld ha.s not yet discovered a. principle -for regulating human. relationship that can supersede Christianity. , ,u

entries.content:
-Tli.e evil ejfeds of heresy. " But if ye bite· and devour .one ,another, ta.k<3 heed that ye be not consumed one of another." · • • I. HERESY GENDERS BITTER DISPUTES. victims to pieces till nothing is left. "Dissolution is the da.ughter of dissension " ~Nazianzen). entries.title: GAL 5:16–18
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The life and warfare of the Spi,rit in the soul. This importani passage suggests a comprehensive view of the Spirit's work in the believer's life. I. 'fHE WORK OF THE SPIRIT IN THE l!ELIEVER. 1. "Walk in the Spirit." Nothin"' could be more descriptive of the natural effect of the spiritual change produced i~ regeneration. 'l'he new-born child soon discovers symptoms of activity. The languiLge of the passage reminds us: (1) Of our dependence on the Spirit. It is not enouO'h tli'at we begin the Divine life; we must maintain it through all its stages and expe~iences. 'l'he exercises of a believer are only effectual by the Spirit. (2) It implies wnsistency. Our life must be in harmony with the mind of the Spirit. His will must be our constant guide. "Therefore grieve not the Holy Spirit." "The fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth." Only thus can we walk in the Spirit. (3) It. implies progress. If we walk, we make progress in our journey. "Enoch walked with God!' 2. Led by the Spirit. This implies an entire surrender of ourselves to the authority and guidance of the Spirit. The traveller in a strange land must follow his guide. So the believer is led by the Spirit with the Word, which is the chart of his journey through life. The term implies, not an isolated act of the Spirit, but a continuous help provided through all parts of a believer's life. JI. THE REASONS BY •WHIOH WE ABE HERE URGED TO MA.INT AIN OUR DEPENDENCE UPON THE SPIRIT. 1. There will be no fulfilling the lusts of the flesh. This is selfevident. The Spirit's guidance will keep us apart from all sinful indulgences, from all earthliness, from all the sins and purposes of the merely natural man. The Spirit and the flesh exclude one another. We shall not trust in our own strength, and so we shall be kept; we shall consult his will supremely, and he will deliver us from the perversities and delusions of our own will. 2. The warfare between the flesh and the Spirit demands eztreme care cm 01/,T part to be always in the Spirit's complete disposal. (1) The conflict in question ts inevitable. Indwelling sin is the calamity of all the people of God. Two powers are at work within· one and the same person. If there were no euoh strife, with the irreconcilable antagonism involved in it, there could be no grace. "The flesh lusteth against the Spirit." It uses the senses to mar the Spirit's power. It presents to the eyes what -will inflame evil passions; it appeals through the ear to appetite; it finds the tongue often too ready to serve its pnrposes. " The Spirit lusteth against the flesh." He is there entrenched within the soul and will not be dislodged. He uses the senses-the eye, the ear, the tongue, the hand, the foot-for the purposes of edification. He conveys thoughts, suggests impressions, and imparts motives, which restrain, guide, and influence the soul. (2) The effects of the conflict. " So that ye cannot do the things that ye would." 'l'his implies that the believer would be free from temptation, but he cannot; he would uninterruptedly serve God, but he cannot; he would be perfect as God is perfect, but he cannot. It is a comfort, after all, to think that on account of the Spirit's operation a believer cannot get doing all the evil he would. (3) This conflict is not without its spiritual advantages. It humbles the believer, by giving him a better knowledge of his sin; it makes him more watchful; it endears the Saviour to him; it commends the riches of Divine grace; it calls into exercise all the graces of the Spirit and all the faculties of bis nature. It makes him long all the more for the rest of heaven. 3. The Spirit's guidance ezempts us from the Law. "If ye be led by the Spirit, ye are not under the Law." The Galatians were for putting themselves again in subjection to Law and forgettinu the free rule of the Spirit. " Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty."" It was necessary to remind them that they were now" dead to that in which they were held" (Rom. vii. 4). It was no longer to them "a Law of sin and death." 11 The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus" made them free from it. How, then, does the Spirit's guidance set them apart from the Law? (1) 'l'he Spirit discovers the hopelessness of acceptance with God through Law. (2) He enables the believer to acquiesce in the blessed discovery that "Christ is the _end of the Law for righ ~eousness to every one that believeth," (3) He enables the believer to regard the Law m a ne\V 0Al,ATIA.N9, 1'.' 274 THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. [cH. v. 1---26.

light, It is now a rule of life. ,The believer does not tremble before it, beoauRo Christ fulfilled it. He delights in it after the inward man. It is to him a Law of liberty now tha.t he is not really under it as a wa.y of justifica.tlon. •:

Yers. 19-21.-Classifiration of the works of the flesh. The picture here exhibited· by the apostle is a frightful a.byss into which he asks us to look down. We have sin in its many varieties pictured in many parts of Scripture (Rom. i. 18-32; 2 Cor. xiii. 2), bnt here we have a most complete account of the works of the flesh. I. THE WORKS OF TilE FLESH. The flesh and the body are not synonymous, The apostle usually speaks of the body in terms <>f respect-unlike QScetics, who .1'.egard it as an enemy, load it with abusive epithets, and try to weaken it with fasts and vigils and penances. He always depreciates and condemns the flesh as a constantly evil tendency in our actual nature. There are sins in this catalogue of an intellectual nature, which cannot be properly ascribed to the body, though they are true works of the flesh. The flesh represents, then, the whole system of corrupt nature, as it brel\ks forth into seventeen different forms of transgression. They fall naturally under four heads. 1. Sins of sensual passion. " Fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness : " the first h~dly reckoned a sin in pagan countries; the second including unnatural sine, which had a fearful import in the East; the third, the impure propensity indulged without check of reason or shame. All three are grouped together elsewhere (2 Cor. xii 21). 2., S'i,ns oj superstition. "Idolatry, sorcery ; " the first referring to the worship of false, gods and of images, which was familiar to the Galatians in connection with idol-feasts; the second to the occult dealings with the world of spirits, so common in .Asia Mi11or. 3. Sins of social disorder. " Hatred, strife, envy, outbursts .of anger, ca"l'.illiqgs, divisions, factions, envyings, murders." It has been remarked.,that there. is a clim11,x in this catalogue of nine evils, for what begins in hatred ends in murder, after ~t has passed. through a whole succession of disturbing a.nd distracting .exper~nces. ,'.rJiey are all violat10ns of brotherly love, representing the selfish, unyielding" bitt.er spirit, .}Vhicbi tQo often enters into reactionary agitations l:>oth!. in Church. 1;1,nd .state. . 4. Individual euesses. "Drunkenness, revellings:" having exclusive relation to ourselves, not· to others. The two terms refeT to scenes o(,g!Ly a.nd wanton dissipation. , , Il. 'Im WORKS OF THE FLESH HAVE AN OVE_l;I.T .CHA,R.6.OTER. They are "manifest.'" The flesh, a.s the sinful principle, breaks out into open acts of tr!Lni;gression, which. are manifest a.like to God a.nd man, manifest by the light of. nature and. by the Law of God. We see the history of the flesh in the :whole, record, of. man's P).oral degradation and his resulting misery. These seventeen,SUIS may not all be equally manifest, for some are gross a.nd others more refined,; they ma.y not all be equally heinous in the• sight either of God or of man; and many_ of them, hateful in God's sight, carry i;io brand of social reprobation with man. Yet they a.re,a.11 me,nifest, open, tangible proofa, of a life at enmity with God. . - III. THE APOSTOLIC wABNING, "They who practise such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." 1. The kingdom of God, founded by Christ, is a. holy kingdom, and consists of those who have entered it by regeneration, who are led by the Spirit, who are heirs of the promise, who a.re "made meet for the inheritance of the saints in light." 2. Transgressors prove their want of meetness f9r·it; they find no enjorment in it; it ha.s no attraction for them ; for these works of the flesh are altogether mconsisteut with the character of the kingdom of God. . IV. THE NECESSITY THAT EXISTS FOB REPEATED WARNINGS AGAINST SIN. "I tell you before, ae I have already told you in time past." We need "line uponi!ine, precept upon precept," to deepen the impression of the hatefulness of sin. It is well to convince sinners of their individual sins, that they ma.y be shut up to fly to the Refuge.

entries.title: GAL 5:22
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-" TJ.e fruit of the Spirit." Here we have the picture of a lovely garden., with a.II the choicll&t growths of the Spirit. . I. THE NINE GRACES oF THE SPIRIT. (1) The a.postlti speaks of the nine as constituting the fruit of the Spirit, a.s if to imply that it t~kes all the ,nine, and no mere selection of graces out of them, to form the one fruit of the Holy Spirit. Christian character must be fully and ha.rmoniow,ly -0eveloped. (:~) Mark the difference between the works of the flesh a.p.d the fruit of the Spirit. Sin is our work; the graces are

the Spirit's·growth in ne. (8) The nine gracel'r throW' themselves n~urally into three groups, each group consisting of three-the first !(l"Oilp,· "love, joy, peace," touching our relations to God; the eecond group," long-suffering, gentleness, goodness," touching o,ur relatione to our fellow-men; the- third group, "faith, meekness, temperance'," touching the_ reg_ulation and conduct of our own individual Christian life. 1. Fir_st group. '" Love; joy; peace." They all spring out of the filial relation into which we are broughtiby.faith in dhrist. Love is the tie that binds out hearts to God as our Father; joy is :the glad emotion that springs up after our reconciliation with God ; peace is the summer calm: •that. settles -down upon the soul that has entered into _its rest. Love has been calfed the foundation of the fabric; joy, the superstructure ; peace, the crown of the work. Love has a primary place, for it is " shed abroad in the heart by the Holy Ghost'." •Jot is•dependent upon love, ana may well be called-" joy of the Holy Ghost." It is enshrined in the very· ~eart of lo·ve, It rises and falls, with love itself, like the thin ·thread of n:ietcury in the-thermometer, by the action of the surrounding atmosphere. Peace· is linked with joy "in believing." Peace and joy are the two ingredients of the kingdom of God (Rom. xiv. 17). It is "the peace to which we are called in one body" (Col.. iii. 15), which will keep our hearts and minds in the midst of all worldly agitations. 2. .SeCJJnd group. "·Long-suffering, gentleness, goodness." The first !(l"OUp blends naturally into the second, for there is a near relation between peace and longsutfering. The graces of this group begin with the passive and end with the active, for long-suffering •is the patient endurance of injuries inflicted by others; goodness is an active principle; 'not a mere kindly disposition; while gentleness or kindness is something between the two---:-a principle, however, which tends largely to promote the usefulness and the' comfort of life, lessening the friction that enters more or Iese into all our intercourse with our fellow-men. 3. -Third group. "Faith, meekness, temperance." 'l'hesti•three graces refer to the regulation of Christian life. It is curious to find faith seventh, and not first, in this list of graces. Faith is the root-principle of all graces. It goes before love itself, for it "worketh by love," and it precedes joy and peace, which both spring from our believing (Roin. xv. 13). It has, therefore, been suggested that faith is here taken for fidelity. '!'here is no reason, however, for any departure from its usual meaning. Faith is here regarded, not as the means of salvation or as the instrument of our justification, but as the principle of Christian life, which controls and guides it. Thus faith supplies the strength of self-control that is implied in temperance, and is the secret spring of that meekness which is an ornament of great price. Temperance comes last in the list of grapes, because self-control ,is tqe end of all Christian life. Like the governor in machinery, it adds nothing to the power at work, but it equalizes the power so as to produce a. uniform type of work. II. MARK THE SPECIAL PRIVILEGE THAT ATTACHES TO THESE NINE GRACES. " Against such there ia no Law.". There ·is Law against the seventeen works of the flesh-to condemn them; but there is no,La.w to condemn the nine graces of the Spirit. There is Law to ,restrain the sinner-it exists for .the purposes of t.his restmint-but in the graces of the Spirit there ·is nothing to restrain. They all chime in with the• requirements of the Law, because they radiate from. that love which is the very fulfilling of the Law•.. 'l'hus those·who are led by the Spirit are not under Law.

entries.title: GAL 5:24
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-The distinguishfag feature of ahristianity. It is manifest in the very nature of the case that a. Christian has crucified the flesh by virtue of his union with Christ. Mark hete-- • • I. 'l'HE ·MOST CHARAOTERISTIO DESIGNATION· 8F TRUE BELIEVERS. "They that are Christ's." • The· expression implies (1) .that they are Christ's ·by purchase, (2) by' deliverance, (3) by possession, (4) by dominion. They are not his merely by external profession. It is natural, therefore; that they should manifest the fruit of the Spirit. II. THE MOST OIIARACTERISTIO PART OF 0HRISTIAN LIFE. "They crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts." This points to a past act, to their conversion, in which, by ,virtue of. their union with Christ, they wore baptized bHu his death (Rom. vi. 4 ). 'l'he ,believer is.Cl crucified with Christ" (eh. ii. 19), but hw;, the flesh, with its seventeen ca.tegories of evil, is cl"Uoified likewise: "Our old w.ac.. has been crucified with him" (Rom. vi. 6). 'l'hns the flesh is robbed of its supremacy. 'l'lrns nnion with Christ secures alike our s11lvation from the guilt and the power of sin. "When Christ 2i6 THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. [err. v. l-26.

came in the flesh, we crucified him; when he comes into our hearts, ,he crucifies us." 'l'he flesh, with its passions and lusts, represents vice on its passive and active sides.

entries.title: GAL 5:25
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: -The wnsistency of the Ohri!tian life, If the flesh has thus been crucified we live by the efficacy of the Spirit. "Crucified: . . . nevertheless I live" (eh. ii. 20)'. I. Oua CHRISTIAN LIFE IS DY THE Srm1T. "If we liye by the Spirit." This life consists in the knowledge of God, in his love, in his favour, in his illlage. l.. It is m·iginated by the Holy Spirit. We are dead in trespasses and sins; it is the Spirit which giveth life. He is "the quickening Spirit" (John vi. 63); "a Spirit of life" (Rom. viii. 2). 2. It is maintained by the Spirit. "We live by the Spirit." , •.• He abideth with us." II. Oua CHRISTIAN WALK IS DY THE SPIRIT, "Let us also walk by the Spirit." There must be a principle of life before it can become manifest in the outward conversation. There must be a correspondence between the outward walk and the inner standard. The walk here referred to points to something very orderly and deliberate, like. the walk of soldiers marching in rank. This "·alk includes (1) the guidance of the Spirit ~Rom. viii. 14); (2) the support of the Spirit (Eph. iii. 16); (3) the drawings of the Spirit: "So that ye walk after the Spirit" (Row. viii. 1, 4); (4) the growth of the character in all the fruit of the Spirit (ver. 22). .

entries.title: GAL 5:2–12
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Falling from grace. Paul in tbe present section exposes the legal and ceremonial spirit as a fall from the moral magnificence of grace. It has been well said that " it is harder to abolish forms than to change opinions. Ceremonies stand long after the thought which they express has fled, as a dead king may sit on his throne stiff and stark in his golden mantle, and no one come near enough to see that : ihe light is gone out of his eyes and the will departed from the hand that still clutches the sceptre." Circumcision was such a form, and against its improper use Paul has all through this Epistle to protest. 'l'he thought of the present section is elevating and sublime. Let us follow the outline. L PAUL HERE IMPLIES THE MORAL MAGNIFICENCE OF SALVATION BY GilA0E. (Vers. 4, 6.) For when we consider how this plan of salvation turns our minds away from self to God in Christ, giving all the glory to the Saviour and taking all the blame to self, we see that it is morally magnificent. Self-confidence is destroyed, .and confidence in Christ becomes all in all. 'fhe whole 11phere of activity is illumined by devotedness to him who has lived and died for our redemption.. Gratitude thus is the foundation of morality, and all idea of merit is put out of sight. The more the gospel is studied as a moral system, the more marvellous and magnificent will it appear. This will further exhibit itself if we consider what the worlcing principle of the gospel is. It is, as Paul here shows," faith working through love" (ver. 6, Revised Version). .,And faith is the mightiest factor in the world's progress. Suppose that faith were supplanted by suspicion, and men, instead of trustiag one another, lived lives of mutual suspicion, • the world's progress would come spef:!dily to an end. '!'he gospel, then, takes this ~ight,y principle of faith and, tl!rning it tow~rdl, Christ, it secures_love as its practical <lit. v. l.,_26.) 'liltlll FlPIS'l'LE 'rO THf GALATIA?il'El. 277

outcome. Love to God and consequent love to men becomes the law of our lives. All that is lovely is thus evoked, and the system proves its moral magnificence and practical power. ' II. IT IB THE OHARAOTERIBTIO OF LEGALISM TO DEPRECIATE THE CROSS. (Ver. 11.) In n scheme of free grace the cross of Jesus Christ is central and all-important. How could S\!lfish hearts be emancipated from their selfishness, ha:d not the Holy Spirit the cross of Christ to move· them? The cross is the self-sacrifice of incarnate love, and the grandest appeal of all history for self-sacrifice in return. It is, moreover, a fact and not a ceremony; a fact which bears no repetition, and which stands in its moral grandeur alone. But legalism comes in to depreciate if possible its moral value. The insinuation is thrown out that circumcision is essential to the efficacy of the cros~ . .The cross is made out to be a mere adjunct to the Jewish ceremonial. Its offence ceases. It is no such instrument of self-sacrifice as it was intended to be. The brav" apostle who preaches "Christ crucified" as the only hope of salvation is persecuted for doing so, and the whole legal band arrays itself against him. It is thus that the legal spirit depreciates and dishonours the Crucified One. III. ALL THIS.IMPLIES IN THE LEGAL SPIRIT A FALL FROM GRACE. (Ver. 4.) This is the key of the present passage. The soul, which so depreciates the cross as to go away and to try to save itself by ceremonies, has fallen from a moral grandeur into deepest selfishness. Christ profits in nothing the soul who is bent on saving himself. The _righteousness of Chlist, whic_h is unto all and upon all them that believe, cannot consist with the self-seeking and self-confidence which self-righteousness implies. We must choose our saviour and adhere to him. If our saviour is to be ceremony, which is only another way of sayin!!: that our saviour is ourselves, then we may as well renounce all hope of.salvation by Christ. We sever ourselves from Christ when we seek to be justified by the .Law (Revised Version). We have descended in toe scale of motive; we. have taken up·the selfish plan; we have" fallen away from grace." IV. PAUL ANTICIPATES THAT HIS EXPOSURE OF LEGALISM WILL CURE THE GALATIANS OF IT. • (Ver. 10.) •He believes that legalism will be destroyed and rooted up by laying bare its real meaning. The leaven will not be allowed to spread. It is most important in the same way to be meditating constantly upon the magnificence of the gospel system a~ a moral system. Thus shall we prize it more and more, and never think of surrenderi~g· it for any rival and selfish system.-R. M. E.

entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
...!.15.-1?!e Uberty of .love. 'Having shown the magnificence of the gospel system, Patil no'? proceeds to define that freedom which it secures. It is not licence, but love, which it induces; .and love nqt only fulfils the Law, as legalism does not, but nlso prevents the bitter strife which l_egalism ensures. We have the following points suggested :- I. THE DIS'.l'IN,C'.J'ION BETWEEN LICENCE AND LIBERTY. (Ver. 13.) The grace which has freed us 'from the legal spirit lias not endowed us with a liberty to live licentiously. The liberty it gives is totally distinct from licence. Licence is liberty to please ourselves, to humour the flesh, to regard liberty as an end and not a means. But God in his gospel gives no such liberty. His liberty is a means and not an end; it is liberty to live as he pleases, liberty to love him and love men, liberty to serve one another by love. We must guard ourselves, th~n, from the confusion of mistaking licence for liberty. . H. LoVE IS THE REAL LinERTY. (Ver. 13.) As 11, matter of experience we never feel free until we have learned to love. When our hearts are going out to God in Christ, when wo have at his cross learned the lesson of philanthropy, wheu we have felt our obligation to God above and to mai;i below, then we are free as air and rejoice .in freedom. Then we refus~ licence as only freedom's counterfeit, for we have learne,l a more excellent way.. We cannot imagine a loveless spirit to be free. Ile may achieve an outlawry, but he is not, cannot be, free. III. LoVE rs THE REAL FULFIL\IIBNT OF THE LAW. (Ver. 14.) The lcgalists in their \ittle system o,f self-righteousness spent 'their strength upon the mint, the anise, and tfie cummin ; ,vhile the weightier matters of the Law-righteousness, judgment, and faith-,,-were nealected. Ceremonies and not morality became their concern. 'l'he tithing of pot-h~rbs would entitle them to Paradise. In contradt to all this, Paul shows 2T8 THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS, .[err. v. 1-:-:26.

that Christian love, which Is another name for liberty, .fnlfilir the demands of .La;w. The mee.ning of the commRndments published from Sinai was love. '!'heir essence is love to God and love to our neighbour, as well as to our "better self." Hence the gospel thro~ no slight on Law, but really secures its observance. '!'he.whole system turns on love as the duty and the privilege of existence. While the Law is, '.therefore, rejected as a way of life, it is accepted as a rule. Saved thro~1gh the .merits.and grace of Christ, we beta.ke ourselves to Law-keeping con araore. We rElcognize in Qod the supreme object of grateful love; we recognize in our neighbour the object of. QUJ,' love for God's sake and for his own sake; and we honour the Law of God as "hply and just and good." The whole difference between the legal spirit and the.gospel spirit is that in the one case Law is kept in hope of establishing a.claim; in ~he other it is kqp~ ~ token of our gratitude. The motive in the one case, being selfis)l, destroys t.he. higli standard of Law. It fancies it can be kept with considcrabl13 ~empleteness, whe.reas it is kept by the best with constant and Jnanifold sqortcoming.. The motive. in the other case, being disinterested, secures such attachment· to ,the Law, because it has been translated int-0 love, that it is kept with increasing ardou~ ,nd success:', Slaves will never honour Law so much as freemen. • , ,J . , • IV. LOVE IS THE TRUE ANTIDOTE TO STRIFE AND DIVISION, (Ver. 15.) · The ritu~l- istic or legal spirit into which the Galatians had temporally fallen manifested itsel( in strife and bickerings. 'l'his is, in fact, its natural outcome. For.'if men are straining every nerve to save themselves by punctilious obs13rvan~ pf qeremoriies, •they will come of necessity into collision. It is an emulation of a, selfish diafacter,' . H Cl!,lj.not be conducted with mutual consideration.. As a matter o~ fact, organizations pervaded i:!y the legal Rpirit are but the battle-ground of conllicting'parties.' 'Bu'tlove comes'to ,Jet all right again. Its genial breath makes summer in society .and takes wintry isol~ti~n :wd .self-seeking all away. Mutual consideration secuf'il"s. harmony';.ild .swial P,rt:>gre~s. 'Instead of religious people becoming then..the butt of the world's scorn by .r.~11s9n of their strife and divisions, they become the world's wonder by reasqn of their unity,l!-nd peace. It is, love, therefore, we are bo.und to cultivate. Then shaU concord and. ·11,11 its myriad blessings come into the Church of God and' the world be subdued b!)for~ it~ -R.M.E. • • • '

entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-Christian :progress r~aliied throug"/,, \intag~rdsm, • We Triu.st not ~uppose, however, that the love which God gives us as our liberty cao. work 'out its will without experiencing opposition. Opposition we know it will meetin. the world of selfish men; but Paul here points out the antagonism. it meets wfthin ou,r own personalities. The flesh antagonizes the Spirit. Love .does riot get its ~~n sw~et· way as often as we would. Self becomes a battle~ground, arid. God, contends 'wi~h tlie flesh.for the supremacy of the soul. So violent is the contention that the flesh is. actually "crucified with its affections and lusts.". We are introduced, the~e(ore, to, the law; of Christian progress which, because of our sinful natur,e, has to be through antagonizing the sinful tendencies in the interest of love. Observe- I. Sn. LEADS MAN TO. FALL OUT WITH.· HIKSELF•. (Ver. 17.). _As UJlma.nn has beautifull v said, ":Man forms a unity, which. is, however, only the 'foundation or that higher unity which is to be brought about in him, as. a being niade i!} the Divi~e image, by means of co=union with God. G;odlike in him-that is, the mind-acquiesces in the Divine order of life, and g~verns the ,vhole being in conformity. therewith.· But when he pas once severed hn:nself from the true centre of his being, that is, from God, thep also do,es that ,element of his being, his mind, whlch is akin to God, and which was intetJ.9-e~ to b?· ihe connecting and all-deciding centre of his personal life, lose its central..au~, dommant position· he c~seH to be lord. of himself and of his own 'iiature; ·the vanous powers w~ich U:a.ke up his complex n~ture begi~. ~ 'carry on,' ~~~h for. i~~elf, ~n indepehd~nt existence; the flesh llll!tetb a.garnet tbe spirit, and the s,:_,mt wages a frmtjess war with the flesh (ver. 17); sinful desire becomes dominant;· and while the man seems to be iII the enjoyment of all imaginable libertf, he :has lost the .only true 'llbert;y- aild ba1 tn, V, 1-26.] THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS.

become a slave to himself; for' whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin' (John viii. 34; Rom, vi, 16-23). He is the dependent of self; and being thus the slave of self, he is also the slave of ple'asure, and of all those objects which it requires for its satisfaction." Man becomes. thus a distracted manifold, instead of a God-centred unity. II, THE SPIRIT OF CHRIST ANTA<lONIZES THE DISTRACTING TENDENCIES AND REDUCES MAN TO A UNITY AGAIN. The way in which we are United in heart and being is by havin,g Jesus Christ pressed resistlessly upon our attention. Faith realizes in Christ not only a. perfect personal Ideal, but also a Saviour on whom man may evermore depend, "'l'he Christ of Christendom is not simply a Master to be loved and revered ; he is a Saviour to be leaned upon. His followers are to have that profound sense of their own weakness and sinfulness which renders them sensitive to the purifying and reforming influences that,radiate from the personality of Jesus. Without this, their love for the ideal would lead. to no practical results; it would be merely an resthetic sentiment, expending it/lelf in a vague and fruitless admiration. But combine the two and you have tne most effective, reforming influence. that the world has ever known." Christ is not only the unifying element in Church life, but in the individual life as well. He fuses all the distracted faculties into a glorious unity, and makes man his own master instead of his own slave, , Hence, to quote the writer last referred to, "Christianity alone among all religic,ns maintains: a constant antagonism to the special tendency which controls tb~ nature of its followers.", Ill.• BUT POSITIVE FRUIT IS PRODUCED BY THE A1''TAGOY.IZING SPIRIT AS A GLORIOt'S SET-OFF TO THE WOR;KS OF THE FLESH WHICH HE.DESTROYS. (Vera. 19-24.) Religion is not to be regarded, as a negative thing, contenting itself with antagonisms, but has positive and ID,Ost important fruits. It is not a system of severe repressions, but a system full of ,stimulus towards a better and fuller life. It does not merely forbid "fornication, uncleanness," etc., under th_e penalty of exclusion 'from the kingdom of God, but it produces ~• love, joy, peace, lqng-suffE1rin,g, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,. meekness, self-control." What a catalogu~ of.virtues! What a contrast to the works of the flesh! Thus is man restored to something like his true and better self. The gospel of Christ is not a weary round of prohibitions, but is a glorious system of positive attainment, in a Divine life, which is loving, joyfu), peaceful, and humane to its deepest depths. IV. AGAINST BUCH BPIBITUALLY MINDED ONES THERE CAN BE NO LAW OF CONDEMNA- TION, (Vers. 18-23.) • Law,,when, translated into love, becomes light. God's com- µiandments are not grievous to the loving soul In the keeping of them there is a great reward. Hence the ,Law presses heavily arid hardly upon no loviD,g spirit. ." There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the ~esh, but after the Spirit'' (Rom. viii. 1). It is to such a blissful experience we are asked to come.-R. M., E.

entries.title: GAL 5:2–12
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content:
-0ircumcision. I. PAUL SOLEMNLY PUTS BEFORE THE GALATIA.~S THE TRUE STATE OF THE CASE. "~ehold, I Paul say unto you, that, if ye receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing." Commencing with an arresting word, he introduces bis own name with all the solemnity of oath-taking, witness-bearing. " Behold, I Paul say unto you." What the weight of his testimony is directed against, is their submitting to circumcision. This was whattheJudaizing teachers were aiming at,and,seeing that they were making false representations, he declares to the Galatians, as if their destinies were at stake, the real state of the case. For them, Gentiles, and at the instigation of the Judaizers, to submit to circumcision would be eJ:cluding themselves from all advantage by Christ. It was either circumcision or Christ with them. There was no middle ground for them to take up. There was no submitting to circumcision and clinging to Christ at the same time. If they submitted to circumcision, they must make up their minds to forego all that they b11d hoped for from Christ. 1. How he malces it out that circumcision u;cluded them from Ghrist. (1) Oircumcisirm implies an obligation to do the whole Law. "Yea, I testify again to every man that receiveth circumcision, that he is a debtor to.do the whole Law." Again does he clear his conscience by el}litting his solemn testimony. '.l'his testimony was more particularly <lirected to every man among them that, under the influence of the Judaizers, had any thought of submitting to circumcision. The &postle, as it were, takes him aside, and 280 THE EPISTLE 'rO 'l'B~ GAtATIANS.

ea:11e~tly ~nd aITeclionately_ w9:rns him. Let him consider what he is doing. He is b_nngmg himself m!der ob)1p:at1on to do the whole Law, and that personally, with this risk attached, that, 1f he fails to do the whole Law, he comes under its curse. (2) Doing the whole Law excludes fi·om Christ anil grace. "Ye are severed from Christ ye who would be jastified by the Law; ye are fallen away from grace." The apostle t~kes the doing of th6 whole Law to be equivalent to the working out of the tvhole of their justi- :fication. That was necessarily to the entire exclusion of Christ. There was nothin"' left for him to do. His work was made of none effect. 'l'hey were severed from Christ and all the benefit of his work. They were thus fallen away from grace. Formerly they stood upon the merits of Christ, they had their Surety to answer for them; now they had themselves, immediately and fully, to answer to God for their Law-keeping. 2. .'J'!ie case of Christians stated. (1) The expectancy of faith. "For we through the Spmt by faith wait for the hope of righteousness." The thought in its simplicity is that we hope for righteousness. This can only be the righteousness on the ground of which we are justified. There is a difficulty in this being presented as future, when it can be immediately and fully enjoyed. Some attempt to get over the difficulty by supposing the meaning to be the hope that belongs to righteousness, i.e. the hope or et1:rnal life. B1;1t that is attaching a not very obvious meaning to the language. If we thmk of justifying righteousness as future, the reference can only be to the vindication of its sufficiency on the day of judgment, and further to the establishing of our personal interest in it on that day. The latter reference especially seems borne orit by the associated language. \Ve are represented as in the att.itude of expectancy. We wait for the hope, i.e. now the realization of the hope of righteousn:ess. This expectancy being based, so far as God is concerned, in the work of the Spirit on our hearts, and so far as we are concerned, in the exercise of faith, is based in reality. But' being based at the same time in that which is not completed, it partakes of imperfection. We are not so sure as those Jndaists were who rested on the fact of''their being circumcised. We are not so absolutely sure as we shall be when judgment has been pronounced in our favour. We are confident that the righteousness of Christ 'will be shown to be all-sufficient as the ground of Justification. And we hope, more or less confidently, according to the operation of the Spirit in our hearts and the working of faith,'that it will be shown that we are possessors of that righteousness. (2) The energy <,>f faith. "'For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth anything, nor uncircumcision·; but faith working through love." The apostle here does not take so high ground with regard to circnmcision. He had forbidden the Galatians to submit to circumcision, on the ground that it would exclude them from Christ. Here he puts circumcision on a level with uncircumcision, as availing nothing within the Christian sphere. Neither is what avails baptism, which has taken the place of circumcision. The outward form is a matter of indilference, unless as it is connected with the inward reality. Whnt must ever be demanded is, as the representation is here--faith, and not a dead faith, but, according to the conception of Paul as well 1'8 according ·to the conception of James, a faith that is operative. And the energy of faith goes out in love.. There is, as we are taught here, a blessed harmony between these two gr~ces. lf we believe that not only God is, but that he is inexhaustible Goodness, we must be drawn out in love towards him. And if we believe that the .Son of God condescended. to become man and devoted himself for us, we must be impelled oU:t beyond ou·rselves towards the good of others. . • IL CERTAIN BEARINGS OF THE CABE ON THE GALATIANS. 1. They were hindered in a good career. "Ye were running well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?" (1) Points in a good career. (a) That it be directed to a right end. This is brought out; in connection with their obeying the truth. 'l'hei~ caree~ in heathenism was vitiated by their being involved in error. 'l'he true idea ?f hfe had n~t bten revealed to them. But when they obeyed the truth they took Christ to be then· end and undertook to shape their career according to the rules of Christ,.' And .that iij necessary to the commencement of a good career. (b) That'it be· comm,enced early. If the Galatians did not commence in early life, yet they commenced as soon as au opportunity in providence was presented to them, and so far they can be cited as an .,xample of commencing early. It would have been a great advantage to th.em to have been taught and moulded as Christians in youth. There would not have been OR. V. 1-26.) 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE G-ALA'fJANS. 281

their heathen educatic,n to unlearn and undo. The laws of association and habit would have been working all along in their favour. And there would have been more time in which to advance to excellence and usefulness. (c) That it be pursued with enthu- Biasm. In the Galatians the warm Celtic temperament was warmed under the influences of the cross. It was this especially that called forth the admiration of the apostle. They did rnn well; among his converts none had displayed greater enthusiasm in the Christian race. (d) That U be pursued with steadiness. It was with regard to this that there was dan11er to the Galatians. Would they continue in their ardent attachment to the gospel? Would time cool their ardour, or would it be transferred to some other doctrine? Especially would they continue steadfast in the face of hindrances that made trial of them? It was that which was now being tested. (2) Hindrances. There are rocks and weeds which are put as hindrances in the way of the farmer cultivating the soil. There are difficulties to be overcome in connection with every worldly calling; We need not wonder, therefore, at there being difficulties in connection with the Chiistian calling. It is only by conquering difficulty after difficulty that we gain the heights of excellence. The greatest difficulties are those which arise from ourselves, from our own weak and treacherous hearts. But we are referred more here to hindrances which arise from others. "Ye were running well; who did binder you?" Jn the word which is used there is an allusion to breaking up roads, by destroying bridge8, raising barriers. There is suggested, by opposition, a representation of what our duty is to our fellow-men. We are to act as pioneers, clearing the way before others by levelling high places, filling up hollows, throwing bridges across rivers. We are to act towards them so that they shall have not only no temptation to fall, but every help to well-doing. And when there are those·who throw obstacles across our path we are not to feel annoyed, as though we had only to deal with them. But we are to feel that God is making trial of us through them. And therefore we are not to succumb, but to persevere in the face of obstacles. Thus out of the eater shall come forth meat; out of our hindrances shall cdme forth the manly virtues. 2. It was not God who was seeking to persuade them to be circumcised. "This persuasion came not of him that calleth you." Persuasion may mean eith_er the state of being persuaded or the act of persuading. 'l'he latter seems more in keeping with the context. The course to which the J udai~ers would have persuaded the Galatians would have been, in its consequences, disobedience to the truth. They would not attempt, we may suppose, to get them to set aside the cross. _Their policy was rather to get them to add circumcision to the cross. This persuasion came not of him.that called them. It was not in accordance, either with the idea that was in the Divine·mind in calling them, or with the idea that was in their own ,minds in choosing the calling, which was in both cases making Christ everythin,g in the road to everlasting haJ;>piness. It did not come from above, from the God who saved them and called th~m to e:verlasting glory, but it came lrom beneathfrom the enemy of mankind. 3. Be.was· afraid of the spread of error among them. "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump." On the one hand, the Judaists, in order to gain their point, woul<l be inclined to minimize its importance. On the other hand, the Galatians might think the Judaistic teaching had made very little way among them. The apostle puts them on their guard by telling them that a little leave11 leaveneth the whole lump. This saying also occurs in 1 Cor. v. 6. The reference there is to a. case of gross immorality in the Corinthian Church. By tolerating such immorality, there would be danger of the whole Corinthian Church being lowered in its moral tone and practice. So by the introduction of a little J udaistic leaven, such as the toleration of the circumcision of a single Gentile convert, there would be danger of the Christian communities of Galatia becoming Judaistic, i.e. commuuities upon which the blessing of God would not rest, from which the Spirit of God would depart. And so a little leaven of carelessness in the household, in companionship, leavens the whole lump. 4-. Be had confidence in them that they u:ould remain unchanged. "I have confidenco to you-ward in the Lord, tbut ye will be none otherwise minded." He had confidence that they would not change from 1\ Christian to. a J udaistic way of thinking, ills confidence was not founded on reports recei vecl re:~anling them. For these,• as we have seen, threw him into a slate of perplexity. llut ho had co116.dence to them-ward in the Lord. He had confidence in the use uf ~ppointed means. He had confidence in the power of prayer. He had prayed to God ou 282 THE EPISTLE TO mE GALATµNs. [on. ,., 1-26.

their behalf, that they might be none otherwise minded. He had confidence in brin~ing proper representations before their minds, llS he had endeavoured .to do. Ho had con- fidence especially in the great Read of the Church making use or the means in the interests of the Gala.tian Churches and of the whole Church, 6. The trouble, would bear Ms ;'udgment. -Freedom smtained by the Spirit. I. UsE 01" CHRISTIAN FREEDOM. •• For ye, brethren, were called for freedom." Paul, having wished the Judaizing teachers ?ff Galatian soil, justifies the strength of bis wish. They would have led the Galatians mto bondage, but God had called them for freedom. He makes e. distinction between the possession of freedom and the use of freedom. He had been under the necessity of making prominent their possession of freedom in contending against the Judsists; he would, however, remind them, as brethren, that there was responsibility connected with their use of freedom. It is thus that be slides into the lllore_practical part of th~ Epistle. l. Dangers of freedom. " Only use not your· freedom for an occasion to the· flesh." By the flesh, which here becomes a leading word with the apostle, we are· not to understand our corporeal nature. Nor are we to understand by it depraved tendency in connection with our corporeal nature. But we are to ·understand by it depraved tendency as a whole, extending to our higher nature as .well as to our· lower nature, It is true that in this depraved tendency our lower nature has the preponderance. And that is the reason why the whble goes by the name of flesh. Bnt the constant element in depravity is not sense, but it is self as opposed to God and to the good of others. The admonition of the apostle, then, is, not that we abstain from all bodily gratification, as though sin were seated in the body, nor simply that we abstain from all fleshly sin, but that we abstain from all selfish gratification. .The Galatians had been called for freedom, i.e. for ultimate and complete freedom ; they wero not, with their first experiences of freedom, or with their strong realization of it as against J udaistic error, to imagine that they were free to indulge the flesh. That is what, as free, we must be on our guard against, if we wonld not fall back into bondage, if we would come to the goal of our freedom in Christ.. Let us not turn our· liberty into licentiousness. 2. The binding of freedom. (1) Love binds the free; !' But through love be servants one to another." As it is self in the flesh that lfa,ds to .abuse of freedom, so it is love that determines the right use of freedom.. Love is. gqi~g out beyond self. It is that which binds us in service to another. The Galatians wer~ free fr.im Jewish bonds only to put on the bonds of Chri8tian love. So it is true tliat we are free from the bonds of guilt only to bind ourselves in service one to another. Thus to balance our freedom-there is the bondage of love. (2) The whole I,,aw is fuifUled in Zove to our neighbour. "For the whole Law is fulfilled in one word, ev~n in thi~; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The one word here is the summary of the ,second table of the Law. The quotation is from Lev. xi.L 18. It appe3:rs,· from "neighbour" there followina upon" children of thy people," that the neighbotit of the Jew was his fellow-Jew. Christ has taught us to regard as our neighbour every !)DC who is in need, temporal or spiritual. When we are commanded to love o·ur neighbour as ourselves, it is implied tha.t it is a right thing to love ourselves. There is a true self-love.: We are to love ourselves intensely. It does not appear that we can be too much ID earnest about our own well-being. \Ve are to love ourselves rationally. We ar~ not to seek. only a section of our interest, but we are to seek our true interest as a whole. In these respects our love to our neiO'hbour is to resemble our love to ourselves. We are to love our neighbour in the same i~tense manner. His good is as much to God as is our own good. And in all ways in which we can advance his good we arE) to be as much in earnest about it as though we were advancing our own. We are to lo~e our neighbour iµ. the same mtional manner. We may love intensely and yet be guided by reason. We are not to seek only part of our neighbour's good. To give as much time and attention to our nei""hbour's business as to our own would not ordinarily be for his good, nor would it be fair to one in comparison with another. Circumstances may arise. iu y.,hich ~uty may point to sacrifice for another, even to the extent of life. Let us, t~en,fove Olli", ne1g~- bour as we love ourselves, both intensely and rationally. The teaclnng of the apostle 1s that he who has obt;erved the second table of the Law (as summarized) ha.s fulfilled the whole Law. Surpri~e has been expressed why there should be no referell!e t? the ti.r~t table of the Law. But the reason is obvious. He who has only gon~ the length of the :first table has not fulfilled the whole Law. Our love to God must be carried to com- pleliou, in our loving our neighbour Wl ourselves. According to tho thought of the

Apostle John, we only properly love our Father-God, whom we do not see, when we love our brother-man whom we see. (3) There is disaster at the opposite pokfromlove. "But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another." The languag@ is ta.ken from wild beasts. The fact of the Galatians being thus warned may be explained partly by their excitable Celtic temperament. They are warned of what they might expect the consequences to be. None would come off victors, but they would be consumed one of another. In such biting and devouring there is a large consumption of. time. • There is distraction from useful work. There is sometimes the consumption of mea11s in litigation. There may be the consumption of life in brawls. There is always• the consumption of good feeling, and, along with that, there is the consumption of the richer elements of the spiritual life. II. 'l'HE FLESH AND THE SPIRI'I'. 1. The Ohristianruleis walking by the Spirit. "But I say, Walk by the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh." 'l'he apostle calls attention to a point to which he advances in the subject he has in hand. This jg laying down the Christian rule as between the flesh and the Spirit. In the flesh, or our depraved nature, there is lust or desire for sinful gratification in some form or another. How.are we to be delivered from this, so that it shall not be ful6lled? The way is positively to follow the leading of the Spirit. The idea. is not that we are to follow t.he·tendencies of our renewed nature. That is missing the personal aspect of the leading. The Spirit, indeed, renews the nature, and excites within it holy desires which seek for gratification. But the Spirit gives personal guiding, especially in and by.the reason and conscience in connection with the Word. And as a Guide he is allsufficient. He is an internal Guide. He throws all the light that we need upon the character of desires and actions, upon the path of duty. And he affords timeous guidance. For whenever we are disposed to turn from the straight path to the right hand or to the left, it is then that we hear his voice behind us, saying," This is the way, walk ye in it." 2. The Ohristian rule isfounded on a contrariety between the flesh and the Spirit. "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are contrary the one to the other; that ye may not do the things that ye would." 'l'he lust ~xcited within the flesh is against the desire excited by the Spirit; the desiro excited by the Spirit is against the lust excited within the flesh. This conflict of desires is necessary. For the flesh and the Spirit are contraries. They represent depraved self and God. 'rhey are as far apart as light and darkness. What is true of the one, then, cannot be true of the other. What the one moves toward in desire, the other necessarily moves against. Of this conflict 'of desires we are conscious in our own experience. When the Spirit impels to good, the flesh opposes ; when the flesh impels to evil, the Spirit opposes. Thus in two ways we cannot do the things that we would. And we have in this conflict of desires, e.s free beings, to determine whether the Spirit or the flesh shall have the dominion of our .hearts. 3. The ahristian rule excludes regulation by the Law. "But if ye are led by the Spirit, ye are not under the Law." The Spirit is an allsufficient Guide. His regulation renders unnecessary all other regulation. He regulates within, and that is bett_er than outward regulation. He regulates in cor.nection with all circumstances that a.rise, e.nd that is better than having the rule to apply for ourselves. Heis a timeous monitor, warning when the danger arises, and that is better than being dependent on memory. 4. There is contrast in the manifestations of the flesh and the Spirit. (1) The works of the flesh. We are to understand manifestations of depravity, e.nd concrete manifestations e.s distinguished from abstraci qualities. Eveu when. the abstract word is used, it is in the plural, with the effect of giving it a concrete character; not the feeling of wrath, but separate exhibitions of wrath; not the feeling ofjealousy, but acts or workings of jealousy. (a) What they are. "Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these." Before enumerating them the apostle describes them as manifest, i.e. easily distinguishable or glaring. It me.y be pointed to as a proof of depravity that vocabularies have more words descriptive of forms of sin than words descriptive of forms of holiness. Under the fruit of the Spirit he gives e. list of nine. But under the works of the flesh his list extends to fifteen, properly sixteen. And the word translated" which" implies that he did not profess to give an exhaustive list-it. wonld have been easy for him to have added other instances. This comparison is con- firmed by the relative number of words for sins and graces employed in Scripture. (a) Sina of uncleannesa. "Fornication. uncleanness, lasciviousne.s.'' What is illicit: ii:t ·idolatry is tbe use ot images to represent the unseen powers. What is illicit; in sorcery (literally, '.' phannac_v" ) is the use of drugs, potions, and other things,• with the idea that· they:c~n rntluence the uneeen powers to produce love or ha.'tred, prosperity or adversity. In strife the variance, mlllY be slight; in acts of jealousy there is more deep-seated variance. · "Wraths, :factions." The former describes outbursts of anger.
