-Sowi11g and rea,p;,ng. The Galatilme appear to have been niggardly in their contributions for the support of their Christian teachers (ver. 6). St. Paul warns them that such conduct will tell against themselves (see Prov. xi. 24). The prin- ciple on which he bases his admonition is one of deep significance and wide application. .l\o doubt the apostle wished it to be impressed upon hie readers in all its bearings ~ well as in relation to the particular case that led him to mention it. L IT I8 A LAW OF NATURE THAT TBB REAPING SHALL OOBBESPOND TO THE BOWING, L This is part of the general law that, other things being equal, the same cause always produces tM sa,me effect. There is no known exception to the law of .causation; there is no possible evasion of it. We see it plainly working in human affairs. The eternal constancy of nature assures us that the consequences of which certain •conduct is known to be the cause will undoubtedly follow. 2. The special' law of sowing antl reaping is that the product of the harvest will be the SOHM in kind as the seed so_wn. Tares will never produce wheat, nor wheat tares. But each seed reproduces its own kind. This is seen in human affairs. Commercial industry tends to commercial wealtb., intellectual study to a state of intellectual culture, etc. It iB vain to think that money will buy refinement or that learnmg is the road to wealth. Each pursuit has its own consequences in accordance with its own nature. IL Tms LAW APPLIES TO SPIRITUAL BOWING AND REAPING. 1. Here the future depends on the past and present by a certain law of causation. No words could more plainly assert that our conduct is shaping our own fate; and these are not the words of St. James, but of St. Paul! and they occur, of all places, in the Epietle,to the Gafatians, where the doctrine of justification by faith is most vehemently asse:rted I Moreover, they are not addressed to Jews still under the Law, nor to heathen who have not yet availed themselves of the privileges of the gospel, but to Christians w.ho have come into the justification by faith, as it is to Christians that St. Paul says elsewhere, •~ We. shall all stand before the judgment-seat of God" (Rom. xiv. 10). , We are here reminded that the future consequences of conduct are, natural, not adventitious-that they are ea.used by what we are and do, that they flow of their owli accord . from ,our lives, and are not assigned from without by any arbitrary dee~. ,We' simply, reap what our own sowing has produced for UB. 2. In spiritual things there is a corraporulence between what is sown and what· is reaped. (1) Sowing to the flesh produces its own natural harvest-corruption. The mere animal life, the life .of worldly interests, the life of the lower self, is itself a life of corruptible. things. Its soil and nourishment are earthly and cannot outlast death. ,When the grave opens all is lost. Even before death thieves steal, and moth and rust eat into the •treasures, The &0ul itself, too, is corrupted by such a life. Its faculties are diBSipated and decay. aay. It descends to the evil state of moral rottenness and death. (:~) Sowing to the '>pirit produces its own harvest of ete~l ~e. Spiritual things _are eternal t~~gs. Treasures in heaven are beyond destroymg mfluences. In proportion as the spmtual within us is cultivated. we have what will outlast death and what no grave will ever claim. .Already we have an eternal life in living in the things• that are spiritual and therefore eternal Money goes, but faith remains; the pleasures of the senses pall upon us, but the peace of God never fails ; self-seeking leads to !iisllatisf!LCtiou, thll lovu of Guel 8UStaip.g us with undying interest5, (IU, Vt, 1--18.J THE EPISTLE TO TlIE GALATIANS. 341

III. THIii KNOWLEDGE OP SUCH A LAW OF SOW'INIJ AND REAPING JS A WARNING AGAINST JNSJN0EBJTY. It ie vain to shut our eye8 to it. Natnre is pitilessly inexorable, and here we are considering a law of nature which is as rigid as the law of gravitation. Deception may avail with men, bnt here we have God's action, and no Aubterfuge can escape his detection. There is a sort of irony on our petty schemes and contrivances In the calm, sure way in which the laws of the universe work out their issues, totally regardless of what we may imagine or pretend. Yet we are In danger of self-deception. 1. The harvest ie delayed. The result is not the less certain, however, on that acconnt. Seeds found bnried with Egyptian mummies thousands of years ago when sown now bear fruit after their kind, with as little deviation as if they bad been produced la.et harvest. 2. We expect more consequences than the l!!iw of gowing and reaping justifies. Thus we are surprised that bad men should be prosperous in worldly matters and good men unfortunate. • But each reaps as be sows. He who sows to the world reaps worldly gain, with its ultimate corruption. He who sows only to the Spirit bas no right to eitpect more than spiritual returns. His harvest will be eternal life, not money and pleasure.. He gets· just what be sows, only with increase. Finally, how can we reconcile this principle with the gospel of Christ and the doctrine of grace? Simply by seeing that to have a true submissive and obedient faith in Christ is to sow to the Spirit.-W. F. A. •

entries.title: GAL 6:9
entries.author: Edgar Huxtable
entries.content: '- Weariness in well-doing. L THE CONDITION OP WEA RTh'EBS m WELL-DOINO. 1. It is a feeling, not at present a change of action. 'l'be well-doing is continued in spite of weariness. Our moods vary, and we can scarcely be held to be responsible for them. 'l'he essential thing is that we do not cease working. 2. It is very different from being weary o/well-tloing. We !llay grow weary in our work and yet be most anxious for the success of it; •Such weariness is a common condition. How often is the flesh weak while the spirit is willing l How often is the spirit, too, wearily cleaving to the dust, a and pining for Divine inspiration, like the hart thirsting and panting for the waterbrooks ! II. Tri EVIL OF THis CONDITION, 1. It is distressing. The task over which we sing in the freshness of the.morning becomes a. burden to groan under when the evening finds us jaded and worn._ 2. It is likely to make our work defective. We cannot row fast when· the stream turns contrary to us, nor work effectively against the grain. 3. It niay lead to the abandonment of our mission. Weariness may end in despair. If we have no joy in our work we shall be tempted to negligence. III. '.THE CAUSES OF THIS CONDITION. 1. In ourselves. (1) Want of rest. "Come ye aside and rest awhile," said Christ to his disciples in the midst of their busiest lab.ours. (2) Want of 11.ourishment. We grow weary if we work long without food. '!'here is a danger lest the active servant of Christ should neglect his own private prayer and meditation and the quiet inward spiritual sustenance that is so necessary to give vigour and freshness to the external service. 2. Causes in our work. (1) Monotony and drudgery. How much of our work has no glow of romance and no inspiration of heroism about it! The soldier grows tired of camp service, though he would put forth tenfold exertions in the excitement of battle without feeling weary. (2) Lack of results. It of~n looks. as though we were labouring in vain. Now, futile toil is of all toil the most. wearying. IV. THE REMEDY -FOR THIS WEARINESS. 1. If it comes from our own habits a.nu conclitions, see that we have the rest and nooriilhment that our souls need. We must be more with God in prayer. Natural bodily rest may be needed too. A good holiday may be the best cure for a weariness that sadly troubles the soul of a conscientious toiler. 2. If the weariness comes from our work, (1) remember that Christ is watching ua, so that the commonest drudgery done for his sake becomes a. noble service and will receive 11s wartn an approval as the most brilliant achievement-nay, a more kindly recognition, seeing \.hat it was more trying to discharge the lowly duty with full fidelity• and (2) remember that the harvest, though delaye,l, will surely be reaped in Jue tim'e,-then "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy."-W. F. A.
